ELA.overview: ELA 8 pairs close reading of classic stories, The Outsiders, founding-era and abolition speeches, Douglass's Narrative, American poetry, The Diary of Anne Frank and A Midsummer Night's Dream with writing in every genre and grammar (verbals, voice, mood). Read each text yourself before the week, read key passages aloud together, and always ask 'Where does the text say that?' Keep 20–30 minutes of independent reading daily and preview mature content noted in each week's prep.

weeks.prep: Read 'The Tell-Tale Heart' yourself first (about 2,200 words; free on Project Gutenberg; LibriVox has an audio version). Parental preview: the narrator murders and dismembers an old man — described briefly but vividly. Print a reading-interest survey; help the child choose an independent reading book.
misconceptions: Taking the narrator's claims of sanity at face value. Ask: does how he says it (frantic dashes, repetition, the obsession with the eye) match what he says?
Confusing gerunds with present participles. Test: if the -ing word can be replaced by 'it' or 'something,' it is a gerund (noun).

days.guide: Have the child complete the interest survey, pick an independent reading book (daily 20–30 minutes all year) and write a one-page 'reading life' reflection. Then read a short Poe biography together and ask what in his life (loss of his mother and wife, poverty) might show up in dark stories.

questions.q: Name two facts about Edgar Allan Poe's life.
questions.a: Examples: he was orphaned young and raised by the Allan family; he lived 1809–1849; his young wife Virginia died of tuberculosis; he is credited with inventing the detective story and wrote 'The Raven.'

days.guide: Read the story aloud (or play LibriVox) while the child follows and marks each place the narrator insists he is not mad. Pause after the first paragraph and ask what kind of person talks this way.

questions.q: How does the story open, and what is the narrator trying to prove?
questions.a: 'True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?' He is trying to prove he is sane by how calmly and carefully he planned the murder.

questions.q: What is his motive?
questions.a: He says he loved the old man and wanted no money; it was the old man's eye — 'the eye of a vulture.'

days.guide: Model the claim–evidence–explanation pattern with one example, then have the child write a paragraph with three pieces of evidence of unreliability and how it builds suspense. Check understanding with: "Give one piece of evidence the narrator is unreliable." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence the narrator is unreliable.
questions.a: Examples: he says the disease 'sharpened my senses' and that he 'heard all things in the heaven and in the earth'; he murders over an eye; he hears a heartbeat after the man is dead.

questions.q: How does unreliability build suspense?
questions.a: Because we can't trust his perceptions, we wait anxiously to see how his frantic mind will betray him — and it does when he confesses.

days.guide: Teach: a gerund is an -ing verb form used as a noun. Find 5 in the story, then the child writes 8 sentences using gerunds as subject, direct object and object of a preposition.

questions.q: Identify the gerund and its job: 'Reading at night was the narrator's habit.'
questions.a: 'Reading' is a gerund used as the subject.

questions.q: Is 'running' a gerund in 'The running dog barked'?
questions.a: No — it describes 'dog,' so it is a participle (adjective).

days.guide: Give the reading and roots quiz (see key), then have the child give a 2-minute oral summary using words such as 'unreliable narrator' and 'suspense.' Finish by asking: "What does 'acute' mean and what root does it contain?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What does 'acute' mean and what root does it contain?
questions.a: Sharp or keen; acu- 'sharp' — the narrator claims his hearing is acute.

weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz (1 point each): 1) What does the narrator hate about the old man? His 'vulture' eye — pale blue with a film over it. 2) How many nights does he look in before acting? Seven; he kills him on the eighth. 3) Where does he hide the body? Under the floorboards. 4) Who comes to the house? Police officers, after a neighbor heard a shriek. 5) Why does he confess? He believes he hears the old man's heart beating louder and louder and thinks the officers are mocking him. 6) acu- means sharp (acute, acupuncture); dis- means not/apart; -ous means full of (nervous, furious). Evidence-paragraph rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear, arguable claim; at least two accurate, embedded quotations; explanation that connects each quotation to the claim; 3 = claim and evidence with thin explanation; 2 = evidence summarized rather than quoted or loosely connected; 1 = opinion without evidence. Proficient claim example: 'The narrator's frantic insistence that he is calm proves he is not.'

weeks.prep: Read 'The Monkey's Paw' (three parts). Print a plot diagram. Parental preview: a son dies in a machinery accident; the ending is eerie.
misconceptions: Thinking foreshadowing is the same as prediction. Foreshadowing is the author's hint; a prediction is the reader's guess based on it.
Dangling modifiers ('Walking home, the paw felt heavy'). The noun right after the participial phrase must be the one doing the action.

days.guide: Read Part I together; child lists every warning about the paw and predicts the first wish's result. Before moving on, ask: "What warnings does Sergeant-Major Morris give?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What warnings does Sergeant-Major Morris give?
questions.a: He says a fakir put a spell on it to show that fate rules people's lives and those who interfere with it do so to their sorrow; the first owner's third wish was for death; he throws it on the fire and says 'Better let it burn'; and he warns, 'If you must wish, wish for something sensible.'

questions.q: What does Mr. White wish for?
questions.a: Two hundred pounds.

days.guide: Finish the story; child completes a plot diagram and marks the peak of suspense (the knocking at the door). Check understanding with: "How does the first wish come true?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: How does the first wish come true?
questions.a: Herbert is killed in the machinery at Maw and Meggins, and the company pays £200 as compensation.

questions.q: What happens with the last two wishes?
questions.a: Mrs. White makes her husband wish Herbert alive; a knocking comes; Mr. White uses the third wish (implied to wish it away) and the road is empty when she opens the door.

days.guide: Model how one line of dialogue reveals character and moves the plot; the child does 3. To check, ask: "What does 'Better let it burn' reveal?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What does 'Better let it burn' reveal?
questions.a: Morris knows the paw's danger from experience and wants it destroyed, which raises the reader's dread and pushes Mr. White to rescue it.

days.guide: Teach present (-ing) and past (-ed/-en) participles as adjectives. Child combines 10 sentence pairs and fixes 3 dangling modifiers.

questions.q: Fix: 'Clutching the paw, the wish was made.'
questions.a: 'Clutching the paw, Mr. White made the wish.'

questions.q: Combine: 'The old man shook. He dropped the paw.'
questions.a: 'Shaking, the old man dropped the paw.'

days.guide: Timed response (25 minutes) on foreshadowing, then the roots quiz. Before moving on, ask: "What does 'credulity' mean and how does it fit the story?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What does 'credulity' mean and how does it fit the story?
questions.a: A readiness to believe; the Whites move from mocking the paw to believing in it.

weeks.assessment_key: Constructed response rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear answer that Jacobs plants warnings to make readers dread the wishes, with 2–3 specific examples (Morris throwing the paw in the fire and saying 'Better let it burn'; the previous owner's third wish was for death; Herbert's joke that he never expects to see the money; the face Herbert sees in the fire), each explained; 3 = two examples, thin explanation; 2 = one example or plot summary; 1 = off-topic. Roots quiz: cred- = believe (credible, incredulous); fid- = faith/trust (fidelity, confide); -ulous = inclined to (credulous = too ready to believe).

weeks.prep: Read 'The Gift of the Magi' (short). Make a three-column irony chart (situational, verbal, dramatic).
misconceptions: Calling any coincidence 'irony.' Situational irony is when the outcome is the opposite of what is expected.
Putting opinions in an 'objective summary.' Remove words like 'sad,' 'beautiful' or 'I think.'

days.guide: Read the story; child tracks each sacrifice and what the reader knows that characters don't. Check understanding with: "What does each character sacrifice and buy?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What does each character sacrifice and buy?
questions.a: Della sells her hair (for $20) to buy a platinum fob chain for Jim's watch; Jim sells his watch to buy her a set of combs.

questions.q: How much money does Della have at the start?
questions.a: One dollar and eighty-seven cents.

days.guide: Teach the three ironies; child sorts 10 examples from the three stories and explains effects. To check, ask: "What type of irony ends 'The Gift of the Magi'?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What type of irony ends 'The Gift of the Magi'?
questions.a: Situational — each gift is useless because of the other's sacrifice.

questions.q: Where is dramatic irony in 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
questions.a: We know the body is under the floor while the officers chat calmly, increasing tension.

days.guide: Model an objective summary (who, what, outcome, no opinion). Child writes one plus a theme statement with two quotations.

questions.q: Why does O. Henry call Jim and Della 'the magi'?
questions.a: Though their gifts are 'foolish,' they gave the greatest gift — sacrificing their treasures out of love — so 'of all who give gifts these two were the wisest.'

days.guide: Teach infinitives (to + verb) as noun, adjective, adverb. Child writes a paragraph using gerund, participle and infinitive.

questions.q: Label the infinitive: 'Jim came home to give Della her gift.'
questions.a: 'to give' — adverb (tells why he came).

days.guide: Give the verbals/irony quiz; discuss which ending is most effective. Check understanding with: "Which ending has situational irony in all three stories?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Which ending has situational irony in all three stories?
questions.a: All three: the narrator betrays himself; the wish for money brings death; the gifts cancel each other.

weeks.assessment_key: Verbals quiz example: identify gerund/participle/infinitive in 'Della decided to sell her hair' (infinitive, noun as object), 'Selling her hair took courage' (gerund, subject), 'The waiting husband came home' (participle, adjective), 'She had $1.87 to spend' (infinitive, adjective) — 1 point each. Theme statement: proficient = a complete sentence that is a universal idea (e.g., 'True love is shown through sacrifice, which matters more than the gifts themselves'), supported by two quotations such as the narrator calling the couple 'the wisest' and 'the magi.'

weeks.prep: Read 'The Most Dangerous Game' (1924, public domain). Print a story map. Parental preview: a man hunts humans; violence including the deaths of a dog and a servant.
misconceptions: Confusing internal and external conflict. Internal = inside the character's mind (fear, doubt); external = against another person, nature or society.
Ending a twist story with 'it was all a dream.' Twists should be set up by earlier clues.

days.guide: Read to Rainsford's arrival at the chateau; mark imagery of ominous mood. To check, ask: "What ominous details appear near Ship-Trap Island?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What ominous details appear near Ship-Trap Island?
questions.a: Sailors' superstition about the island, the 'moonless Caribbean night' with darkness 'like moist black velvet,' a gunshot, and a scream.

days.guide: Finish the story; chart Rainsford's conflicts and Zaroff's values. Finish by asking: "What does Zaroff hunt and how does he justify it?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What does Zaroff hunt and how does he justify it?
questions.a: Humans — sailors he lures with false lights; he says 'Life is for the strong' and calls his victims 'scum.'

questions.q: How does the story end?
questions.a: Rainsford hides in Zaroff's bedroom, defeats him, and 'had never slept in a better bed' — implying Zaroff died.

days.guide: Collect 5 suspense techniques with examples. Before moving on, ask: "Give a suspense technique from 'The Monkey's Paw.'" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Give a suspense technique from 'The Monkey's Paw.'
questions.a: Foreshadowing (Morris's warnings) or the cliffhanger knocking at the door.

days.guide: Plan a 2–3 page suspense story with a story map, including a planted twist clue. Check understanding with: "What makes a twist fair?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What makes a twist fair?
questions.a: Earlier clues make it surprising but believable when re-read.

days.guide: Draft the opening (≥400 words) with a hook, sensory details and a foreshadowing clue. To check, ask: "What is the 'hook' of 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What is the 'hook' of 'The Tell-Tale Heart'?
questions.a: The narrator's frantic denial of madness in the first line.

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric for plan + opening (4 levels): 4 = plan shows narrator, clear conflict, rising action and a twist with a planted clue; opening ≥400 words with a hook, sensory details and one foreshadowing clue; 3 = all parts, weaker clue or details; 2 = plan or opening incomplete; 1 = little planning.

weeks.prep: Revision and editing checklists. Print 'The Open Window' by Saki for Friday (do not let the child read it early).
misconceptions: Revising only for spelling. Revision means changing content and structure; editing is fixing errors.
Punctuating dialogue wrong: the comma or period goes inside the quotation marks.

days.guide: Finish the draft with dialogue and a resolution. Finish by asking: "Punctuate: she said I'm coming" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Punctuate: she said I'm coming
questions.a: She said, "I'm coming."

days.guide: Revise using the checklist. Before moving on, ask: "How do short sentences affect pacing?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How do short sentences affect pacing?
questions.a: They speed it up and create tension.

days.guide: Edit and publish. Check understanding with: "Correct: 'Look out' he yelled." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Correct: "Look out" he yelled.
questions.a: "Look out!" he yelled.

days.guide: Child reads aloud; listeners identify the twist and clues. To check, ask: "What should listeners be able to name?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What should listeners be able to name?
questions.a: The twist and at least one clue that foreshadowed it.

days.guide: Cold-read 'The Open Window' and answer questions (key). Finish by asking: "Who is the unreliable storyteller in 'The Open Window'?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Who is the unreliable storyteller in 'The Open Window'?
questions.a: Vera, the niece.

weeks.assessment_key: Published narrative rubric (4 levels: plot/conflict, pacing, dialogue, conventions). Cold-read test answers for 'The Open Window': 1) Vera (the niece, 15) tells Framton that Mrs. Sappleton's husband and two brothers went shooting three years ago and drowned in a bog, and the window is left open for their return. 2) When the men return, Framton flees in terror. 3) Vera then invents a story that he fears dogs because he was hunted by pariah dogs in a cemetery on the Ganges. 4) Irony: situational — the 'ghosts' are real men and the reader, like Framton, was fooled. 5) Point of view: third person; we don't learn Vera's lie until the end. 6) Last line: 'Romance at short notice was her speciality' — 'romance' means made-up stories.

weeks.prep: Get a library copy of The Outsiders; read chapters 1–3. Parental preview: gang violence, smoking, drinking, a teen is beaten; later a stabbing and deaths.
misconceptions: Treating Greasers as 'good' and Socs as 'bad.' Track how Hinton shows both groups suffering.
Thinking passive voice is always wrong. It's useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

days.guide: Read about 1960s Tulsa and Hinton writing the novel as a teen; predict conflicts. Before moving on, ask: "How old was S. E. Hinton when she began The Outsiders?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How old was S. E. Hinton when she began The Outsiders?
questions.a: About 15–16; it was published in 1967.

days.guide: Read chapters 1–2; start the character chart. Check understanding with: "What happens to Ponyboy in chapter 1?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What happens to Ponyboy in chapter 1?
questions.a: Socs jump him walking home from the movies; his brothers and friends rescue him.

days.guide: Read chapter 3; journal entry on 'Things are rough all over.' To check, ask: "What does Cherry mean by 'Things are rough all over'?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What does Cherry mean by 'Things are rough all over'?
questions.a: Socs have problems too — emotional ones — even though they have money.

days.guide: Teach active vs passive voice; rewrite 10 sentences. Finish by asking: "Rewrite in active: 'Ponyboy was jumped by the Socs.'" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Rewrite in active: 'Ponyboy was jumped by the Socs.'
questions.a: 'The Socs jumped Ponyboy.'

days.guide: Quiz; discuss whether the groups are more alike or different. Before moving on, ask: "Name one thing Ponyboy and Cherry share." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Name one thing Ponyboy and Cherry share.
questions.a: They both like watching sunsets.

weeks.assessment_key: Chapter 1–3 quiz: 1) Narrator: Ponyboy Curtis, 14. 2) Brothers: Darry (oldest, works two jobs, acts as guardian) and Sodapop. 3) Johnny was badly beaten by Socs before the story. 4) At the drive-in Johnny tells Dally to leave Cherry and Marcia alone. 5) Cherry says 'Things are rough all over.' 6) Ponyboy runs away after Darry slaps him. Discussion rubric: cites text, responds to others.

weeks.prep: Read chapters 4–6 and 'Nothing Gold Can Stay' (8 lines). Parental preview: Johnny kills Bob; a church fire injures Johnny.
misconceptions: Thinking 'gold' means money. In Frost's poem gold is the early, fleeting beauty of nature — and of youth/innocence.
Confusing allusion with illusion.

days.guide: Read chapter 4; analyze the park. Check understanding with: "What happens in the park?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What happens in the park?
questions.a: Socs try to drown Ponyboy in the fountain and Johnny stabs and kills Bob.

questions.q: Who helps them flee?
questions.a: Dally gives money and a gun and sends them to an abandoned church in Windrixville.

days.guide: Read chapter 5 and the poem; annotate imagery. To check, ask: "What does 'Nature's first green is gold' mean?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What does 'Nature's first green is gold' mean?
questions.a: New leaves first look golden; the poem says beauty and innocence don't last.

days.guide: Read chapter 6 together or independently. Ask the child to find where Ponyboy, Johnny and Dally act differently than their 'hood' reputations suggest, and write how the fire changes how they see themselves.

questions.q: What happens at the church in chapter 6?
questions.a: The church catches fire (likely from their cigarette) while schoolchildren are inside; Ponyboy and Johnny go in and save them; a falling timber badly injures Johnny, and Dally pulls them out.

questions.q: How does the fire change how the boys see themselves?
questions.a: They act as heroes rather than 'hoods'; Ponyboy realizes Dally and Johnny are capable of gallantry, and the newspapers call them heroes.

days.guide: Explain allusion (a reference to a well-known work). Child explains how Gone with the Wind and the Frost poem deepen the theme.

questions.q: Why does Johnny connect the Southern gentlemen in Gone with the Wind to Dally?
questions.a: They rode into sure death gallantly; Johnny sees Dally's loyalty and courage that way — which foreshadows Johnny's own sacrifice.

questions.q: How does the Frost allusion deepen the theme?
questions.a: It frames youth and innocence as 'gold' that fades, which becomes Johnny's message to Ponyboy to 'stay gold.'

days.guide: Model a theme statement as a complete sentence about life, not one word. Child writes a theme paragraph about 'staying gold' with two pieces of evidence and commentary.

questions.q: Who recites 'Nothing Gold Can Stay,' and when?
questions.a: Ponyboy, while he and Johnny watch the sunrise from the church.

questions.q: Turn the topic 'innocence' into a theme statement.
questions.a: Example: 'Innocence fades as people face hardship, but holding on to wonder and kindness lets a person stay "gold."'

weeks.assessment_key: Theme paragraph rubric: 4 = theme stated as a universal idea (e.g., innocence is precious and fleeting but can be kept by holding on to goodness), two pieces of evidence (Frost's 'Nothing gold can stay,' Johnny's 'Stay gold, Ponyboy'), explanation.

weeks.prep: Read chapters 7–9 ahead. Parental preview: the rumble (a gang fight) and Johnny's death in chapter 9 are emotional; be ready to talk about grief. Note: Johnny's line 'Useless...fighting's no good' actually comes in chapter 9, right after the rumble; in chapter 8 he says 'Sixteen years ain't long enough.'
misconceptions: Thinking the Greasers' rumble victory resolves the conflict. Johnny's dying words call fighting useless; nothing really changes.
Believing passive voice always weakens writing. It can hide the doer on purpose (e.g., to show confusion in the chaos of a fight).

days.guide: Read chapter 7. Ask the child to list everything Randy says to Ponyboy and decide what it proves about the Socs.

questions.q: What does Randy tell Ponyboy?
questions.a: He's sick of the fighting, Bob's death has shaken him, and he won't go to the rumble — evidence that Socs suffer and question the violence too.

questions.q: How do the newspapers describe Johnny and Ponyboy?
questions.a: As heroes for saving the children from the burning church.

days.guide: Read chapter 8. Discuss Johnny's condition and how it affects Ponyboy (fear, denial, guilt).

questions.q: What does Johnny say about his life in chapter 8?
questions.a: 'Sixteen years ain't long enough' — he realizes he's done so little and wants to live.

questions.q: Why won't Cherry visit Johnny?
questions.a: He killed Bob, whom she cared about.

days.guide: Read chapter 9. Child analyzes the rumble and Johnny's last words.

questions.q: What does Johnny say to Dally and then to Ponyboy?
questions.a: 'Useless...fighting's no good' and then 'Stay gold, Ponyboy. Stay gold.'

questions.q: Why is the victory hollow?
questions.a: Johnny dies right after; the fighting changed nothing important.

days.guide: Child rewrites a short rumble paragraph in active and passive voice and explains which is stronger. Check understanding with: "Rewrite in active voice: 'Ponyboy was kicked in the head by a Soc.'" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Rewrite in active voice: 'Ponyboy was kicked in the head by a Soc.'
questions.a: 'A Soc kicked Ponyboy in the head.'

days.guide: Give the chapters 7–9 quiz (key). To check, ask: "Who wins the rumble?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Who wins the rumble?
questions.a: The Greasers.

weeks.assessment_key: Chapters 7–9 quiz: 1) Newspapers call Ponyboy and Johnny heroes; Johnny's back is broken. 2) Randy tells Ponyboy he's sick of fighting and won't go to the rumble; Bob's death shook him. 3) Cherry won't visit Johnny because he killed Bob. 4) In chapter 8 Johnny says 'Sixteen years ain't long enough.' 5) The Greasers win the rumble. 6) After Dally says 'we won,' Johnny says 'Useless...fighting's no good' and then 'Stay gold, Ponyboy. Stay gold' before dying. Voice rewrite rubric: both versions grammatically correct (2), explanation of which has more impact and why (2) — e.g., active voice ('Darry slammed the Soc') is more vivid; passive can emphasize the victim.

weeks.prep: Read chapters 10–12. Print an essay planning sheet; highlighters. Parental preview: Dally is shot by police.
misconceptions: Writing a thesis that is a fact ('The Outsiders is about two gangs'). A thesis must be arguable and answer 'what does Hinton suggest?'
Choosing quotations only from one part of the book. Require evidence from beginning, middle and end.

days.guide: Read chapter 10; journal entry on Dally's death and Ponyboy's denial. Finish by asking: "Why does Dally get himself killed?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why does Dally get himself killed?
questions.a: Johnny was the one person Dally loved; without him Dally breaks and wants to die, raising an unloaded gun so police shoot.

questions.q: How does Ponyboy react?
questions.a: He insists Johnny isn't dead, then collapses with a concussion and fever.

days.guide: Finish the novel; annotate Johnny's letter and the last line. Before moving on, ask: "What does Johnny's letter say?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What does Johnny's letter say?
questions.a: Staying gold means staying young and seeing beauty; there's 'still lots of good in the world'; tell Dally.

questions.q: What is the circular structure?
questions.a: The final line returns to the first line, showing Ponyboy is writing the book as his theme.

days.guide: Model one weak thesis and one arguable one. Child drafts three and chooses one.

questions.q: Example arguable thesis about growing up?
questions.a: 'Hinton suggests that growing up means seeing past labels like Greaser and Soc to recognize everyone's shared pain.'

days.guide: Child selects 6 quotations across the novel with two sentences of analysis each. To check, ask: "Give a quotation about seeing beyond labels and explain it." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Give a quotation about seeing beyond labels and explain it.
questions.a: 'Things are rough all over' (Cherry) — shows Socs suffer too, challenging Ponyboy's assumptions.

days.guide: Build the outline; give the quiz. Finish by asking: "Who is cleared at the hearing?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Who is cleared at the hearing?
questions.a: Ponyboy.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) After Johnny dies, Dally robs a grocery store and is shot by police under a streetlight, raising an unloaded gun. 2) Ponyboy is sick with a concussion for days and insists he killed Bob. 3) At the hearing Ponyboy is cleared. 4) Johnny's letter (in Gone with the Wind) says there's still lots of good in the world, tells Pony to stay gold, and to tell Dally. 5) Ponyboy decides to write his English theme — the book itself. 6) The last line repeats the first: 'When I stepped out into the bright sunlight from the darkness of the movie house...' Outline rubric: arguable thesis; three body topics with two quotations each; conclusion idea.

weeks.prep: Arrange to watch the 1983 film The Outsiders (directed by Francis Ford Coppola; rated PG) — preview the church-fire and rumble scenes. Have the essay outline ready.
misconceptions: Dropping quotations without introducing or explaining them. Use claim–quotation–commentary every time.
Judging a film only by whether it's 'like the book.' Ask what each change accomplishes.

days.guide: Model one body paragraph: topic sentence, introduced quotation with page number, 2–3 sentences of commentary. Child drafts three.

questions.q: Embed this correctly: Cherry says things are rough all over.
questions.a: As Cherry tells Ponyboy, "Things are rough all over" (Hinton 35). [page number varies by edition]

days.guide: Child writes introduction and conclusion; revises for transitions and active voice. Check understanding with: "What three parts belong in an introduction?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What three parts belong in an introduction?
questions.a: A hook, brief context (title, author, situation), and the thesis.

days.guide: Watch the two scenes; chart kept / changed / cut. To check, ask: "Who directed the 1983 film?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Who directed the 1983 film?
questions.a: Francis Ford Coppola.

questions.q: Why might a film cut scenes?
questions.a: Running time, visual pacing, or focusing the story on action.

days.guide: Child prepares 3 open questions; hold a seminar on whether the film captured the theme. Finish by asking: "Give an open (not yes/no) question." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Give an open (not yes/no) question.
questions.a: 'How does the film use the sunset to show what Ponyboy and Cherry share?'

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test and collect the final essay. Before moving on, ask: "What does 'Stay gold' mean?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What does 'Stay gold' mean?
questions.a: Keep your innocence and ability to see beauty.

weeks.assessment_key: Literary analysis essay rubric (4 levels per trait): Thesis (arguable, answers the prompt); Evidence (≥6 embedded quotations from across the novel, cited by page); Commentary (explains how each quotation supports the claim); Organization (intro, 3 bodies, conclusion, transitions); Conventions (voice, verbals, punctuation). Unit 2 test answers: Greasers vs Socs; Ponyboy narrates; Darry is the oldest brother/guardian; 'Stay gold' alludes to Frost's 'Nothing Gold Can Stay'; Johnny kills Bob to save Ponyboy; theme example: violence and labels hurt everyone.

weeks.prep: Print Patrick Henry's 'Speech to the Second Virginia Convention' (March 23, 1775). Collect 6 ads (print or online).
misconceptions: Thinking any emotional word is pathos and any number is logos. Ask what the appeal makes the audience feel, think or trust.
Confusing mood with tone. Grammatical mood is the verb form (statement, command, question, condition, wish).

days.guide: Teach ethos, pathos, logos. Child labels 6 ads with an explanation each.

questions.q: A dentist in a white coat recommends a toothpaste. Which appeal?
questions.a: Ethos — trust in the expert.

days.guide: Read the speech aloud; annotate rhetorical questions, repetition and appeals. To check, ask: "Give a rhetorical question from the speech." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Give a rhetorical question from the speech.
questions.a: 'Is life so dear, or peace so sweet, as to be purchased at the price of chains and slavery?'

questions.q: How does Henry use ethos in the opening?
questions.a: He respects the patriotism and abilities of those who disagree, which makes him seem fair and trustworthy.

days.guide: Chart claim, supporting claims, evidence; judge soundness. Finish by asking: "What is Henry's central claim?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What is Henry's central claim?
questions.a: The colonies must fight Britain now — 'give me liberty or give me death.'

questions.q: What evidence does he use?
questions.a: British fleets and armies arriving, ten years of failed petitions, and 'the lamp of experience.'

days.guide: Teach the five moods; child labels 10 sentences. Before moving on, ask: "Mood of 'Give me liberty, or give me death!'?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Mood of 'Give me liberty, or give me death!'?
questions.a: Imperative.

days.guide: Quiz; child delivers the last paragraph aloud. Check understanding with: "Which appeal dominates the final line?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Which appeal dominates the final line?
questions.a: Pathos.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) ethos = credibility; pathos = emotion; logos = logic/evidence. 2) 'Is life so dear, or peace so sweet, as to be purchased at the price of chains and slavery?' → rhetorical question, pathos. 3) 'I have but one lamp by which my feet are guided, and that is the lamp of experience' → logos (reasoning from past experience). 4) Label moods: 'Give me liberty' imperative; 'The war is actually begun' indicative; 'Shall we gather strength by irresolution and inaction?' interrogative; 'If I were a delegate, I would vote for war' subjunctive + conditional. Oral delivery rubric: volume, pacing, emphasis on key words, eye contact.

weeks.prep: Print the Declaration of Independence and Gettysburg Address (National Archives transcripts).
misconceptions: Thinking the Declaration's main body is the 'all men are created equal' sentence. Most of the text is the list of grievances.
Using 'was' in the subjunctive ('If I was king'). Use 'were.'

days.guide: Outline the four parts: preamble, statement of rights, grievances, resolution of independence. To check, ask: "What steps does the second paragraph build?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What steps does the second paragraph build?
questions.a: Self-evident truths → governments exist to secure rights with consent of the governed → when government destroys these ends, the people may alter or abolish it.

days.guide: List 10 loaded words and their effect on tone. Finish by asking: "What does 'usurpations' suggest?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What does 'usurpations' suggest?
questions.a: Seizing power illegally — the King looks like a criminal tyrant.

questions.q: Note on 'merciless Indian Savages'?
questions.a: A dehumanizing slur reflecting colonists' prejudice; discuss how loaded language can be propaganda.

days.guide: Close-read the Gettysburg Address. Before moving on, ask: "Give the past-present-future structure." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Give the past-present-future structure.
questions.a: Past: 'Four score and seven years ago' the nation was founded; present: 'Now we are engaged in a great civil war'; future: 'a new birth of freedom.'

questions.q: Example of parallelism?
questions.a: 'government of the people, by the people, for the people.'

days.guide: Teach conditional and subjunctive; child writes 8 sentences. Check understanding with: "Correct: 'If I was in Congress, I would vote yes.'" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Correct: 'If I was in Congress, I would vote yes.'
questions.a: 'If I were in Congress, I would vote yes.'

days.guide: Write the comparison response. To check, ask: "Year of the Gettysburg Address?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Year of the Gettysburg Address?
questions.a: 1863 (November 19).

weeks.assessment_key: Response rubric (4 levels): 4 = explains that the Declaration persuades by moving logically from principles (rights, consent) to evidence (grievances) to conclusion (independence), and the Gettysburg Address by moving past–present–future and parallelism to rededicate listeners; cites words from each; 3 = both texts, thin evidence; 2 = only one text; 1 = summary only.

weeks.prep: Print both versions of Sojourner Truth's 1851 Akron speech (Marius Robinson's report in the Anti-Slavery Bugle, 1851; Frances Dana Gage's version, 1863) and the Declaration of Sentiments (Seneca Falls, 1848). Prepare a short new argument passage for Friday (e.g., a letter to the editor on school start times).
misconceptions: Assuming the famous 'Ain't I a Woman?' text is a word-for-word record. Gage published it 12 years later, added the refrain and a Southern dialect (Truth grew up in New York speaking Dutch); Robinson's 1851 report, written by someone present, is considered more reliable.
Confusing counterclaim with rebuttal. Counterclaim = the opposing view; rebuttal = the answer that weakens it.
Shifting voice or mood mid-sentence ('First read the speech, and then you should annotate it'). Keep one mood: 'Read the speech, and then annotate it.'

days.guide: Read Gage's version aloud. For each 'Ain't I a woman?', the child writes the opponent's claim it answers (women are delicate; women have less intellect; Christ was a man; Eve brought sin).

questions.q: What claim does the first refrain answer?
questions.a: That women must be helped into carriages and over ditches; she says nobody ever helped her, and she has worked, plowed and borne the lash as well as any man.

questions.q: How does she answer 'Christ wasn't a woman'?
questions.a: 'Where did your Christ come from? From God and a woman! Man had nothing to do with Him.'

days.guide: Read Robinson's report and compare line by line. Discuss which is more reliable and why texts differ.

questions.q: Does Robinson's 1851 version contain the refrain 'Ain't I a woman?'
questions.a: No — it is in standard English and lacks the refrain.

questions.q: Why is Robinson's version considered more reliable?
questions.a: He was a friend who was present and published it within weeks; Gage wrote it 12 years later and added dialect and details.

days.guide: Read the Declaration of Sentiments; chart its parallel to the Declaration of Independence (preamble, rights, grievances against 'man,' resolutions). Check understanding with: "How does Stanton revise Jefferson's famous sentence?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: How does Stanton revise Jefferson's famous sentence?
questions.a: 'We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal.'

questions.q: Name one grievance.
questions.a: Women are denied the right to vote (the 'elective franchise'); married women lose property rights; women are barred from most colleges and professions.

days.guide: Teach voice and mood shifts; child corrects 10 sentences and writes a paragraph in consistent active, indicative verbs. To check, ask: "Fix the shift: 'First read the speech, and then you should annotate it.'" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Fix the shift: 'First read the speech, and then you should annotate it.'
questions.a: 'Read the speech, and then annotate it.' (both imperative)

days.guide: Give the new-passage quiz (key). Finish by asking: "Define rebuttal." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Define rebuttal.
questions.a: A response that answers and weakens a counterclaim.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument-analysis quiz rubric (on the new passage, 4 points): names the author's claim (1); identifies the counterclaim the author acknowledges (1); identifies the rebuttal (1); judges whether the rebuttal is convincing with a reason (1). Shifts items: 'If I was mayor, I will fix the roads' → 'If I were mayor, I would fix the roads'; 'Stanton wrote the declaration, and it was signed by one hundred people' → 'Stanton wrote the declaration, and one hundred people signed it.'

weeks.prep: Choose paired articles on one debate (CommonLit or ReadWorks, e.g., cell phones in schools); print a credibility checklist; find a short student debate or TED-Ed talk on the topic.
misconceptions: Thinking a source is credible because it looks professional. Check author expertise, date, purpose and evidence.
Treating any disagreement as a disagreement about facts. Often both sides accept the same facts but interpret them differently.

days.guide: Child reads both articles and annotates each claim and strongest evidence. Before moving on, ask: "What is the difference between a claim and evidence?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What is the difference between a claim and evidence?
questions.a: A claim is the arguable position; evidence is the facts, data or examples that support it.

days.guide: Mark disagreements; label each fact vs interpretation. Check understanding with: "Two articles cite the same study showing test scores rose after a phone ban; one says bans work, the other says other changes explain it. Fact or interpretation?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Two articles cite the same study showing test scores rose after a phone ban; one says bans work, the other says other changes explain it. Fact or interpretation?
questions.a: Interpretation — they agree on the data but disagree about the cause.

days.guide: Apply the checklist to 4 more sources. To check, ask: "A 2009 blog by an anonymous phone seller — keep it?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: A 2009 blog by an anonymous phone seller — keep it?
questions.a: Reject: outdated, no author expertise, commercial bias.

days.guide: Watch the debate; evaluate relevance and sufficiency. Finish by asking: "What makes evidence 'sufficient'?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What makes evidence 'sufficient'?
questions.a: Enough credible evidence to support the claim — more than one anecdote.

days.guide: Child writes claim, three reasons, one counterclaim. Before moving on, ask: "Why include a counterclaim?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why include a counterclaim?
questions.a: Addressing it shows fairness and strengthens the argument.

weeks.assessment_key: Source evaluation chart: each of 4 sources rated on author, date, purpose, evidence and bias with a keep/reject decision and reason (1 point per source); claim statement: arguable claim + three distinct reasons + one named counterclaim (4 points). Example: 'Middle schools should require phones to stay in lockers during class because they distract learning, enable cyberbullying, and reduce face-to-face interaction; opponents say phones are needed for emergencies.'

weeks.prep: Source notes, argument essay template. Print an excerpt of Frederick Douglass's 1852 speech 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?' (often titled 'The Hypocrisy of American Slavery').
misconceptions: Ending with a summary only. A strong conclusion adds a call to action or the stakes.
Citing evidence without explaining it. Every piece of evidence needs 1–2 sentences of reasoning.

days.guide: Model a hook and a clear claim; child drafts intro and two body paragraphs with cited evidence. Check understanding with: "Give a hook type." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Give a hook type.
questions.a: A surprising statistic, a question, or a brief anecdote.

days.guide: Draft counterclaim-and-rebuttal and conclusion with a call to action. To check, ask: "Sentence frame for a counterclaim?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Sentence frame for a counterclaim?
questions.a: 'Some argue that ... However, ...'

days.guide: Revise with you using the rubric; check each piece of evidence clearly supports the claim. Finish by asking: "What should you do with evidence that doesn't support the claim?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What should you do with evidence that doesn't support the claim?
questions.a: Cut it or replace it with relevant evidence.

days.guide: Edit for shifts and commas; publish with MLA works cited. Before moving on, ask: "Where does the works-cited page go?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Where does the works-cited page go?
questions.a: On its own page at the end, alphabetized by author.

days.guide: Cold-read test on the Douglass excerpt. Check understanding with: "What does Douglass say the Fourth of July is to the slave?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What does Douglass say the Fourth of July is to the slave?
questions.a: 'a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.'

weeks.assessment_key: Argument essay rubric (4 levels per trait): Claim; Evidence (cited, credible, relevant); Reasoning; Counterclaim & rebuttal; Organization; Conventions (no mood/voice shifts, commas, works cited). Unit 3 cold-read answers: 1) Claim: the Fourth of July reveals the 'gross injustice and cruelty' of slavery; America's celebration of liberty is hypocrisy while it enslaves millions. 2) 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine' — contrast/antithesis, pathos. 3) 'What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?' — rhetorical question. 4) 'it is not light that is needed, but fire; it is not the gentle shower, but thunder' — metaphor/parallelism arguing that scorn, not calm argument, is needed. 5) Audience: Northern white listeners in Rochester, NY (1852).

weeks.prep: Download the Narrative (Project Gutenberg). Parental preview: whippings, a murder, separation of families, and racial slurs quoted from slaveholders; Douglass describes these to expose slavery's cruelty. Decide how you'll handle the slur when reading aloud.
misconceptions: Thinking the preface was written by Douglass. William Lloyd Garrison wrote it to vouch for the book.
Mixing up Mr. Severe (chapter 2) with Mr. Gore (chapter 4).

days.guide: Read a biography and Garrison's preface. To check, ask: "Why did the book need Garrison's preface in 1845?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Why did the book need Garrison's preface in 1845?
questions.a: Many white readers doubted a formerly enslaved man could write so well; Garrison, a famous abolitionist, vouched for its truth.

days.guide: Read chapters 1–2; annotate birthday and mother. Finish by asking: "How does Douglass describe not knowing his birthday?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: How does Douglass describe not knowing his birthday?
questions.a: He says most slaves 'know as little of their ages as horses know of theirs' — slavery denies basic identity.

days.guide: Read chapters 3–4; chart overseers (Mr. Severe appears in chapter 2).

questions.q: What happened to Demby?
questions.a: Mr. Gore shot him when he refused to come out of a creek; Gore was not punished.

days.guide: Write a purpose paragraph. Check understanding with: "Who is Douglass's intended audience?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Who is Douglass's intended audience?
questions.a: Northern white readers, to win support for abolition.

days.guide: Reading and vocabulary quiz. To check, ask: "Define 'dehumanize.'" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Define 'dehumanize.'
questions.a: To treat someone as less than human.

weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz: 1) Douglass doesn't know his age/birthday — slaves knew as little of their ages 'as horses know of theirs.' 2) He was separated from his mother as an infant; she visited only a few times at night and died when he was about seven. 3) Aunt Hester's whipping was 'the blood-stained gate, the entrance to the hell of slavery.' 4) Mr. Severe was 'rightly named: he was a cruel man.' 5) Mr. Gore shot Demby and was never punished. Purpose paragraph rubric: purpose (expose slavery's cruelty and support abolition), audience (Northern white readers), two pieces of evidence.

weeks.prep: Read chapters 5–8 of the Narrative. Make a punctuation sheet on dashes, commas and ellipses. Parental preview: chapter 8 describes Douglass's grandmother turned out to die alone.
misconceptions: Using an ellipsis to change a quotation's meaning. Omissions must keep the author's meaning.
Using a hyphen (-) where a dash (—) is needed.

days.guide: Read chapters 5–6. Discuss Mr. Auld's warning that learning would 'forever unfit him to be a slave' and Douglass's realization.

questions.q: What did Douglass realize after Mr. Auld forbade his lessons?
questions.a: 'I now understood ... the pathway from slavery to freedom' — literacy.

questions.q: How does Sophia Auld change?
questions.a: She begins kind, but slavery's power hardens her.

days.guide: Read chapter 7; list every learning strategy. Before moving on, ask: "Name three strategies." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Name three strategies.
questions.a: Trading bread with poor white boys for lessons; reading The Columbian Orator; copying letters marked on ship timbers; copying from Master Thomas's copybook.

days.guide: Read chapter 8; analyze the grandmother passage's word choice and tone. Check understanding with: "What happened to his grandmother?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What happened to his grandmother?
questions.a: After serving the family her whole life, she was sent to a hut in the woods to die alone.

questions.q: What is the tone?
questions.a: Bitter, ironic outrage — e.g., she was 'made welcome to the privilege of supporting herself.'

days.guide: Practice dashes, commas and ellipses quoting Douglass in 8 sentences. To check, ask: "When do you use an ellipsis in a quotation?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: When do you use an ellipsis in a quotation?
questions.a: To show words were omitted.

days.guide: Objective summary of chapters 5–8; punctuation quiz. Finish by asking: "What book did Douglass buy at about age 12?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What book did Douglass buy at about age 12?
questions.a: The Columbian Orator.

weeks.assessment_key: Summary rubric: objective, in order, covers Baltimore move, Auld's warning, learning to read/write, the valuation and grandmother. Punctuation quiz example answers: 'Douglass realized that learning was "the pathway from slavery to freedom."' / 'He traded bread—his only payment—for lessons.' / ellipsis used correctly with three spaced dots at an omission.

weeks.prep: Read chapters 9–11 and the Appendix of the Narrative. Prepare a semester review packet and exam: one literary and one informational cold-read passage with questions, 10 grammar items, and a timed essay prompt. Parental preview: the fight with Covey and descriptions of beatings.
misconceptions: Thinking Douglass rejects religion. In the Appendix he separates slaveholding religion from what he calls 'the Christianity of Christ,' which he embraces.
Calling any repetition chiasmus. Chiasmus reverses the order of key words in two parallel phrases (A–B, B–A).

days.guide: Read chapters 9–10 (Thomas Auld, then Edward Covey). Write the chiasmus on the board, draw arrows showing the reversed word order, and ask the child how the sentence's shape mirrors what happens to Douglass.

questions.q: Explain 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.'
questions.a: The reversed order mirrors the reversal in his life: Covey's brutality nearly broke him, but fighting back restored his sense of manhood and self-worth — the turning point of the book.

questions.q: What happened after Douglass fought Covey?
questions.a: Covey never tried to whip him again; Douglass said he was a changed man, determined to be free.

days.guide: Read chapter 11 and the Appendix. Discuss why a book about escaping would leave out how the escape happened.

questions.q: Why does Douglass withhold the details of his escape?
questions.a: Publishing them could endanger the people who helped him and would alert slaveholders to the method, closing that route for others.

questions.q: Where does he settle and what name does he take?
questions.a: New Bedford, Massachusetts; he takes the name Douglass (suggested by Nathan Johnson) and marries Anna Murray.

days.guide: Child takes a practice cold read independently, then checks with the answer key and writes why each missed answer was wrong. To check, ask: "What makes a summary 'objective'?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What makes a summary 'objective'?
questions.a: It reports the main ideas in order without opinions, judgments or 'I.'

days.guide: Quick-fire review of verbals, voice, mood and punctuation (10 items), then plan — but don't write — a timed essay: claim, three reasons, evidence list. Finish by asking: "Identify the verbal: 'Waiting for news, Della counted her money.'" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Identify the verbal: 'Waiting for news, Della counted her money.'
questions.a: 'Waiting for news' is a participial phrase modifying Della.

questions.q: Which mood is 'I insist that he be on time'?
questions.a: Subjunctive.

days.guide: Give the semester exam: cold reads, grammar items and a timed analytical essay (about 40 minutes). Before moving on, ask: "Define chiasmus and give the example from Douglass." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Define chiasmus and give the example from Douglass.
questions.a: A reversal of word order in parallel phrases: 'how a man was made a slave ... how a slave was made a man.'

weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam scoring: cold reads — score with your key (main idea, inference, word meaning, author's purpose, text evidence). Grammar items with answers to use: 1) 'Swimming is good exercise' → gerund (subject). 2) 'The broken paw lay on the floor' → past participle (adjective). 3) 'Douglass wanted to read' → infinitive (noun/object). 4) Rewrite 'The speech was delivered by Henry' → 'Henry delivered the speech.' 5) 'If I were free, I would write' → subjunctive + conditional. 6) Fix 'Running to the door, the knocking stopped' → 'Running to the door, Mrs. White heard the knocking stop.' Timed essay rubric: arguable claim (4), evidence (4), commentary (4), organization (4), conventions (4).

weeks.prep: Narrative, informative essay template. Prepare the Unit 4 test from the questions in the key.
misconceptions: Arguing instead of informing. An informative essay explains a topic with evidence; it does not push the reader to act.
Paraphrasing too closely (swapping a few words). Read, cover the source, write from memory, then check and cite.

days.guide: Hold a seminar: 'Why was reading so dangerous to slaveholders?' Require the child to cite at least three passages by chapter or page, and push back with 'Where does it say that?' Check understanding with: "What is a strong answer?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What is a strong answer?
questions.a: Reading let enslaved people learn about rights and abolition (The Columbian Orator; the word 'abolition'), think critically about slavery, and potentially forge passes; Mr. Auld said it would 'unfit' a slave — knowledge undermined control.

days.guide: Model a controlling idea (not a claim). Child outlines three subtopics with evidence for each.

questions.q: Give an example controlling idea.
questions.a: 'In the Narrative, Douglass shows that literacy was both his path to freedom and a source of painful awareness.'

days.guide: Child drafts, mixing direct quotations with paraphrases and adding page citations. Finish by asking: "Format a parenthetical citation for a quotation on page 37." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Format a parenthetical citation for a quotation on page 37.
questions.a: ..."the pathway from slavery to freedom" (Douglass 37). [page varies by edition]

days.guide: Revise for precise vocabulary and varied sentence openings; edit quotation punctuation. Before moving on, ask: "Fix: Douglass said 'I now understood'." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Fix: Douglass said "I now understood".
questions.a: Douglass wrote, "I now understood...." — introduce with a comma and put end punctuation inside the quotation marks.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test and collect the final essay. Check understanding with: "Who first taught Douglass the alphabet?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Who first taught Douglass the alphabet?
questions.a: Sophia Auld, his mistress in Baltimore, until her husband stopped her.

weeks.assessment_key: Informative essay rubric (4 levels per trait): controlling idea; three subtopics each with quotation and paraphrase cited by page; precise vocabulary; varied sentence openings; correctly punctuated quotations. Unit 4 test answers: 1) Purpose: expose slavery's cruelty and support abolition; audience: Northern white readers. 2) Garrison wrote the preface to vouch for authenticity. 3) Mr. Auld said reading would 'forever unfit him to be a slave' — Douglass saw 'the pathway from slavery to freedom.' 4) He learned by trading bread for lessons, The Columbian Orator, ship-timber letters and copybooks. 5) The fight with Covey was the turning point. 6) He hides escape details to protect helpers. 7) Short analysis of tone in the grandmother passage (bitter irony).

weeks.prep: Print 'O Captain! My Captain!' and 'I Hear America Singing' (Walt Whitman) and 'I, Too' (Langston Hughes) from Poetry Foundation. Choose an unfamiliar Whitman stanza (e.g., from 'Song of Myself') for Friday.
misconceptions: Reading 'O Captain!' literally as a sea story. It's an elegy using an extended metaphor for Lincoln's assassination at the end of the Civil War.
Thinking free verse has no craft. Whitman builds rhythm with repetition, catalogs and parallel lines.

days.guide: Read the elegy aloud. Child maps the extended metaphor: ship = the nation, captain = Lincoln, fearful trip = the Civil War, prize = Union victory/preserved nation.

questions.q: Why does the speaker contrast ringing bells with the fallen captain?
questions.a: The crowds celebrate victory while the speaker grieves — joy and loss collide as Lincoln is killed just as the war ends.

questions.q: What kind of poem is it?
questions.a: An elegy — a poem mourning a death (Lincoln's, 1865).

days.guide: Read 'I Hear America Singing.' Child lists every worker in the catalog and explains the effect of the long, rhythmic free-verse lines. Finish by asking: "Name four workers in Whitman's catalog." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Name four workers in Whitman's catalog.
questions.a: Mechanics, carpenter, mason, boatman, deckhand, shoemaker, hatter, wood-cutter, ploughboy, mother, young wife, girl sewing or washing.

questions.q: What does 'Each singing what belongs to him or her and to none else' suggest?
questions.a: Every person's work and identity is unique and valuable to the nation.

days.guide: Read 'I, Too.' Ask who 'they' are and what the kitchen and the table symbolize. Before moving on, ask: "Who is 'the darker brother'?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Who is 'the darker brother'?
questions.a: A Black American, sent to eat in the kitchen when company comes — excluded from equal place.

questions.q: What will happen 'Tomorrow'?
questions.a: He'll be at the table, and 'they'll see how beautiful I am / And be ashamed' — 'I, too, am America.'

days.guide: Child writes the comparison paragraph with evidence from both poems. Check understanding with: "How does Hughes's first line answer Whitman?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: How does Hughes's first line answer Whitman?
questions.a: 'I, too, sing America' adds a voice Whitman's catalog left out.

days.guide: Give the figurative-language quiz on the unfamiliar stanza. To check, ask: "Define anaphora." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Define anaphora.
questions.a: Repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive lines.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison paragraph rubric (4 levels): 4 = states Whitman's theme (America is made of many workers, each singing 'what belongs to him or her') and Hughes's response (Black Americans are part of that song though excluded, and will claim their seat at the table), with a quotation from each and explanation; 3 = both poems, weak explanation; 2 = one poem; 1 = summary. Figurative language quiz: correctly identifies in the stanza a catalog, anaphora, free verse, the speaker, and any metaphor (1 point each), plus explains one effect.

weeks.prep: Print Dunbar's 'Sympathy' and 'We Wear the Mask,' Lazarus's 'The New Colossus' and Frost's 'The Road Not Taken.' Review the terms Petrarchan sonnet (octave + sestet, turn) and rhyme scheme.
misconceptions: Reading 'The Road Not Taken' as simple advice to be a nonconformist. The poem says both roads were worn 'really about the same'; the speaker predicts he'll later tell it differently.
Marking rhyme scheme by spelling instead of sound. Read the line endings aloud.

days.guide: Read both Dunbar poems aloud. Child explains the caged bird and mask metaphors and how the refrains build intensity.

questions.q: Why does the caged bird sing in 'Sympathy'?
questions.a: Not from joy — 'It is not a carol of joy or glee, / But a prayer that he sends from his heart's deep core' — a plea for freedom.

questions.q: What does the mask hide?
questions.a: Pain and suffering; people 'grin and lie' to survive in a world that won't see their tears.

days.guide: Child marks the rhyme scheme of 'The New Colossus' and finds the turn. Before moving on, ask: "How does the turn change the meaning?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How does the turn change the meaning?
questions.a: The octave contrasts the statue with the conquering Colossus of Rhodes; the sestet gives her voice, welcoming 'your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free.'

days.guide: Analyze structure of 'The Road Not Taken'; debate sincere vs ironic. Check understanding with: "What evidence suggests irony?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What evidence suggests irony?
questions.a: The roads were 'really about the same' and 'equally lay / In leaves no step had trodden black,' yet he predicts he'll say 'with a sigh' that he took 'the one less traveled by.'

days.guide: Child writes the structure comparison citing two poems. To check, ask: "What is a Petrarchan sonnet?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What is a Petrarchan sonnet?
questions.a: 14 lines: an octave (ABBAABBA) and a sestet (often CDCDCD), with a turn between them.

days.guide: Give the form and sound quiz. Finish by asking: "Give an alliteration from 'The New Colossus.'" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Give an alliteration from 'The New Colossus.'
questions.a: 'sea-washed, sunset gates' or 'world-wide welcome.'

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) 'The New Colossus' rhyme scheme: ABBAABBA CDCDCD (Petrarchan sonnet). 2) The turn comes at line 9, when the statue speaks: 'Keep, ancient lands, your storied pomp!' 3) 'Sympathy' refrain: 'I know what (why) the caged bird ...' 4) 'We Wear the Mask' — the mask that 'grins and lies' hides pain (Black Americans' suffering hidden from a hostile world). 5) 'The Road Not Taken' stanzas: 4 stanzas of 5 lines, ABAAB. 6) Define alliteration and personification with examples. Structure comparison rubric: explains how the sonnet's octave/sestet turn shifts from describing to the statue's voice, and how Frost's regular rhyme and the 'sigh' ending create ambiguity; cites both.

weeks.prep: Print Longfellow's 'Paul Revere's Ride' and Poetry Out Loud recitation tips (poetryoutloud.org). Find a brief historical account of April 18–19, 1775.
misconceptions: Believing the poem is accurate history. Longfellow wrote it in 1860 to inspire unity; Revere did not ride alone, did not wait for the lantern signal himself, and was captured before reaching Concord.
Reciting too fast. Mark pauses at punctuation, not at line breaks (enjambment).

days.guide: Read 'Paul Revere's Ride' aloud for its galloping rhythm. Then read a short historical account of April 18–19, 1775, and the child lists three differences between poem and history.

questions.q: What does 'One if by land, and two if by sea' mean?
questions.a: Lanterns hung in the Old North Church tower would signal whether the British were coming by land or by water (across the Charles River).

questions.q: Name two differences from history.
questions.a: Revere arranged the signal for others and was rowed across; William Dawes and Samuel Prescott also rode; Revere was captured and never reached Concord (Prescott did).

days.guide: The child chooses a poem from the unit (or Poetry Out Loud's anthology) and marks a copy with slashes for pauses and underlines for emphasis. Memorize a stanza at a time by reading aloud, covering, and reciting.

questions.q: What is enjambment?
questions.a: A sentence continuing past the end of a line without punctuation — don't pause there.

days.guide: Show a few lines of Whitman's catalog and a rhymed stanza with a refrain as models. The child drafts one free-verse catalog poem and one poem with a rhyme scheme and a refrain.

questions.q: What makes Whitman's style a 'catalog'?
questions.a: A long list of specific people, things or images, often with repeated openings.

days.guide: The child recites the memorized poem for family. Listeners give one specific compliment and one suggestion on volume, pacing or eye contact.

questions.q: Name three recitation qualities.
questions.a: Volume, pacing, eye contact (also articulation and accuracy).

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test on an unfamiliar poem; collect the portfolio. Before moving on, ask: "Define narrative poem." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Define narrative poem.
questions.a: A poem that tells a story with characters and plot.

weeks.assessment_key: Recitation rubric (Poetry Out Loud style, 4 levels): physical presence, voice and articulation, dramatic appropriateness, accuracy (few or no missed words). Original poems: free-verse catalog uses repetition and a list of specific images; rhymed poem has a consistent scheme and a refrain. Unit 5 test: answers depend on the chosen poem; key items — speaker, form, rhyme scheme, two figurative devices with effects, and theme statement.

weeks.prep: Get the play 'The Diary of Anne Frank' (Goodrich and Hackett). Read USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia articles (ushmm.org). Parental preview: Holocaust content — persecution, fear, and the knowledge that most characters die in camps. Preview USHMM videos before showing.
misconceptions: Thinking the play is Anne's diary. It's a dramatization by two playwrights based on it.
Ignoring stage directions. They carry setting, action and mood.

days.guide: Read two or three USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia articles together (Nazi rise to power; the Netherlands; Anne Frank). The child builds a timeline of 8–10 key events from 1933 to 1945.

questions.q: When did Germany invade the Netherlands?

days.guide: Explain acts, scenes and stage directions (italic text describing setting and action). Read Act 1, Scene 1 aloud, including directions, and ask why the play begins after the war ends.

questions.q: How does the play open?
questions.a: November 1945: Mr. Frank returns, broken, to the empty attic; Miep gives him Anne's diary and he begins to read — the action flashes back to 1942.

questions.q: Why open with the ending?
questions.a: The audience knows the outcome, creating dramatic irony.

days.guide: Read Act 1, Scene 2 aloud with assigned parts (you can take several). The child records what each character's first lines reveal about him or her.

questions.q: What do Peter's first actions reveal?
questions.a: Shy, quiet; he arrives with his cat and later tears off his yellow star.

days.guide: Look at photographs (Anne Frank House website), watch a short USHMM video and read an article about the Secret Annex. The child charts what each medium shows best and what it leaves out.

questions.q: Strength of photographs?
questions.a: They show the real place.

days.guide: Give the quiz on historical background and Scenes 1–2; collect the timeline. Check understanding with: "Who gives Anne the diary in Scene 2?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Who gives Anne the diary in Scene 2?
questions.a: Her father.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline (key dates to include): 1933 Hitler becomes chancellor (Jan.) and the Franks begin moving to Amsterdam; 1935 Nuremberg Laws; Nov. 1938 Kristallnacht; Sept. 1939 Germany invades Poland; May 1940 Germany invades the Netherlands; 1942 Jews in the Netherlands forced to wear yellow stars; July 1942 Franks go into hiding; Aug. 4, 1944 arrest; early 1945 Anne dies at Bergen-Belsen; Jan. 27, 1945 Auschwitz liberated; May 1945 war ends in Europe. Quiz: Scene 1 is set in November 1945 with Mr. Frank returning alone and Miep giving him the diary; Scene 2 flashes back to July 1942 as the Franks and Van Daans arrive.

weeks.prep: Read Act 1, Scenes 3–5 of the play. Borrow 'Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl' and choose one entry to compare (e.g., an entry about her mother or about Hanukkah 1942). Note: the names Van Daan and Dussel are pseudonyms; the real people were the van Pels family and Fritz Pfeffer.
misconceptions: Seeing Anne as simply 'rude.' Help the child see a teenager confined for years, testing independence under fear.
Treating tension as only physical danger. Tension also comes from conflicts among the people hiding.

days.guide: Read Scene 3. Child lists Anne's conflicts with Mrs. Van Daan and with her mother, with a line for each.

questions.q: Why does Mrs. Van Daan get angry with Anne?
questions.a: Anne is loud and teasing, pesters Peter, and spills milk on Mrs. Van Daan's prized fur coat.

questions.q: Who arrives at the end of the scene?
questions.a: Mr. Dussel, a dentist, who brings news of deportations and must share Anne's room.

days.guide: Read Scenes 4–5 aloud. Ask the child to mark when the mood shifts from joy to fear in the Hanukkah scene.

questions.q: How does the Hanukkah scene build tension?
questions.a: The joyful celebration and Anne's gifts are interrupted by a noise downstairs — a thief; Peter knocks over a lamp, and everyone freezes, afraid the thief will report them.

questions.q: What happens after Anne's nightmare (Scene 4)?
questions.a: She calls for her father and rejects her mother's comfort; Mrs. Frank is deeply hurt.

days.guide: Read one diary entry and its dramatized scene; list what the playwrights changed and why (stage time, visual action, compressing events). Before moving on, ask: "Why might playwrights combine or invent moments?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why might playwrights combine or invent moments?
questions.a: Plays need visible action and conflict in limited time, so events are compressed or dramatized.

days.guide: Child writes the character analysis of Anne with four quotations. Check understanding with: "Give one trait of Anne with evidence." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Give one trait of Anne with evidence.
questions.a: Optimistic and energetic — she treats hiding as an adventure early on and makes gifts for everyone at Hanukkah.

days.guide: Give the Act 1 quiz (key). To check, ask: "Why must they stay silent during the day?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Why must they stay silent during the day?
questions.a: Workers in the business below could hear them and report them.

weeks.assessment_key: Character analysis rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear claim about Anne's character (e.g., lively, outspoken and hopeful but struggling with her mother and growing up), four accurate quotations from Act 1 with commentary, organized paragraphs; 3 = three quotations; 2 = traits listed with little evidence; 1 = summary. Act 1 quiz: Mr. Dussel, a dentist, joins them and shares Anne's room; Anne clashes with Mrs. Van Daan and with her mother; after her nightmare Anne wants her father, not her mother, hurting Mrs. Frank; during Hanukkah a thief downstairs hears Peter knock over a lamp; Anne makes handmade gifts for everyone.

weeks.prep: Read Act 2, Scenes 1–3. Parental preview: hunger and quarrels intensify; references to arrests and deportations.
misconceptions: Confusing dramatic irony with suspense. Dramatic irony is the gap between what the audience knows and what characters know; it creates suspense or dread.
Seeing Mr. Van Daan's theft as only greed. Discuss how fear and starvation test everyone.

days.guide: Read Act 2, Scene 1 with assigned parts. Ask how Anne's voice in her diary reading has changed since Act 1 and how her relationship with Peter is shifting.

questions.q: How has Anne changed since Act 1?
questions.a: She is more thoughtful and mature, reflecting on growing up and her feelings, and becoming closer to Peter.

days.guide: Read Scene 2. Remind the child that Act 1, Scene 1 told us Mr. Frank returned alone; list moments where characters' hopes are painful because the audience knows the outcome.

questions.q: What does the audience know that characters don't?
questions.a: That they will be discovered and only Mr. Frank will survive — so every plan for 'after the war' feels heartbreaking.

days.guide: Read Scene 3 (the stolen bread). Discuss how hunger and fear push the characters to conflict and how the invasion news changes the mood.

questions.q: What does Mr. Van Daan do and how does Mrs. Frank react?
questions.a: He steals bread at night; she demands that he leave the Annex.

questions.q: What news changes the mood?
questions.a: Miep brings news of the Allied invasion of Normandy (D-Day).

days.guide: Review the claim-evidence-commentary pattern. The child writes the irony paragraph with two examples and explains the dread each creates.

questions.q: Example of dramatic irony?
questions.a: Characters celebrate the invasion news believing liberation is near.

days.guide: Give the quiz on Act 2, Scenes 1–3 and collect the irony paragraph. Finish by asking: "What does Kraler report about a worker?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What does Kraler report about a worker?
questions.a: A worker is suspicious and asking for more money — a threat of blackmail.

weeks.assessment_key: Irony paragraph rubric (4 levels): explains dramatic irony (the audience knows from Act 1, Scene 1 that only Mr. Frank survives), gives two examples (e.g., hope at news of the invasion; Anne's plans for the future; Kraler's report of a suspicious worker), and explains the feeling it creates (dread). Quiz: Scene 1 — New Year's 1944, Miep and Mr. Kraler visit with a cake, Kraler says a worker (Carl) is asking suspicious questions and wants more money; Scene 2 — Anne and Peter grow close; Scene 3 — Mr. Van Daan is caught stealing bread, Mrs. Frank demands he leave, then news of the D-Day invasion brings joy.

weeks.prep: Read Act 2, Scenes 4–5. Arrange to watch selected scenes of the 1959 film 'The Diary of Anne Frank' (directed by George Stevens). Parental preview: the arrest scene and the epilogue revealing the deaths.
misconceptions: Reading Anne's 'good at heart' line as naive. Discuss it as a choice to hold on to hope despite evidence.
Judging the film only by faithfulness. Ask what each director's choice adds or loses.

days.guide: Read Act 2, Scene 4 aloud, including the tense ringing phone and the arrival of the police. The child writes what Anne's 'good at heart' line reveals and why the playwrights placed it just before the arrest.

questions.q: What does 'In spite of everything, I still believe that people are really good at heart' reveal?
questions.a: Anne's hope and faith in humanity, even while persecuted — the play's central theme.

days.guide: Read the final scene. Discuss how returning to November 1945 frames the whole play as Mr. Frank's memory and why he says 'She puts me to shame.'

questions.q: How does Scene 5 connect to Act 1, Scene 1?
questions.a: Both are set in November 1945 with Mr. Frank; the play is framed as his memory of reading the diary.

days.guide: Watch 2–3 selected scenes of the 1959 film with the script open. The child charts what the director kept, changed or added and the effect of each choice.

questions.q: Who directed the 1959 film?
questions.a: George Stevens.

days.guide: Model a theme thesis. The child plans an essay with thesis, three supporting points and two quotations for each.

questions.q: Example thesis?
questions.a: 'Through Anne's choices, the play shows that hope can survive even the cruelest persecution.'

days.guide: Give the quiz on the play and collect the film comparison chart. Review any missed questions with the script.

questions.q: Where did Anne die?
questions.a: Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, early 1945.

weeks.assessment_key: Film comparison chart rubric: ≥4 differences between script and film, each with the effect on the audience (1 point each). Quiz: Scene 4 — the phone rings repeatedly below; Anne tells Peter she still believes people are good at heart; the Green Police/Gestapo arrive; Mr. Frank says they can now live in hope rather than fear. Scene 5 — November 1945, Mr. Frank tells Miep and Kraler that all the others died, Anne at Bergen-Belsen; he reads Anne's line and says 'She puts me to shame.'

weeks.prep: Print Elie Wiesel's 1986 Nobel Peace Prize acceptance speech; select two USHMM survivor testimonies. Find two accounts of the Annex's discovery (e.g., Anne Frank House website and a USHMM article). Parental preview: survivor testimony.
misconceptions: Thinking neutrality is fair. Wiesel argues neutrality helps the oppressor.
Assuming conflicting accounts mean someone lied. Memory, perspective and available evidence differ.

days.guide: Give brief background: Wiesel survived Auschwitz and Buchenwald as a teenager and wrote 'Night.' Read the speech together; the child underlines his central claim and explains in writing why he says neutrality helps the oppressor. Check understanding with: "What is Wiesel's claim?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What is Wiesel's claim?
questions.a: 'We must always take sides. Neutrality helps the oppressor, never the victim. Silence encourages the tormentor, never the tormented.'

days.guide: The child reads two accounts of the August 4, 1944 arrest and lists details that agree and differ. Discuss why accounts differ (memory, sources, date written).

questions.q: What remains unknown?
questions.a: Who betrayed the people in the Annex — it has never been proven.

days.guide: The child picks Miep Gies, Irena Sendler or Chiune Sugihara and takes notes from three credible sources (USHMM, Yad Vashem, a library book), recording source and page for each fact. Finish by asking: "What did Miep Gies do?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What did Miep Gies do?
questions.a: Helped hide the Franks and saved Anne's diary, giving it to Otto after the war.
