weeks.prep: Tape measure; recruit 8 people for arm-span/height (or use a provided dataset); graph paper. Find or make a car age vs value dataset.
misconceptions: Thinking an association proves cause. Arm span doesn't cause height; both relate to body size.
Choosing axis scales that start at 0 and squash the data. Start the axes near the smallest values and mark a break.

days.guide: Measure arm span and height (fingertip to fingertip, arms straight) of 8+ people and record in a table with units. Before moving on, ask: "Which variable should go on the x-axis and why?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Which variable should go on the x-axis and why?
questions.a: Arm span, if we're using it to predict height — the explanatory variable goes on x.

days.guide: Child chooses scales and plots by hand; describe the pattern. Check understanding with: "What pattern do you expect for arm span vs height?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What pattern do you expect for arm span vs height?
questions.a: A positive, roughly linear association — arm span is close to height for most people.

days.guide: Child classifies 8 scatter plots by direction (positive/negative/none) and form (linear/nonlinear), marking outliers and clusters. To check, ask: "What association do you expect between a car's age and its value?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What association do you expect between a car's age and its value?
questions.a: Negative — older cars are generally worth less.

days.guide: Discuss the car data's outliers and possible reasons. Finish by asking: "An old car worth much more than others its age is an outlier. Give a reason." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: An old car worth much more than others its age is an outlier. Give a reason.
questions.a: It may be a classic or collectible car, or exceptionally well kept, so its value rose instead of falling.

days.guide: Quiz: child builds and describes a scatter plot from a 12-row table. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: What does 'no association' look like on a scatter plot?
questions.a: Points scattered with no upward or downward trend.

weeks.assessment_key: Project rubric: 4 = labeled axes with units and consistent scales, all points plotted accurately, correct description (direction, form, strength, outliers/clusters); 3 = minor plotting or labeling errors; 2 = plot present but description missing or wrong; 1 = incomplete. Quiz on the 12-row table: accept the description that matches the data, e.g., 'strong positive linear association; one outlier at (x, y).'

weeks.prep: Spaghetti strand or clear ruler, graph paper, last week's arm-span data, Desmos.
misconceptions: Drawing a line that connects the first and last points. A good line of fit has about as many points above as below and follows the trend.
Trusting predictions far outside the data. Extrapolation can give impossible results (e.g., a negative car price).

days.guide: Lay spaghetti on the scatter plot to fit a line. Compare with a second placement and ask which is closer to more points.

questions.q: What makes a good line of fit?
questions.a: It follows the trend with points roughly balanced above and below and small distances from the points.

days.guide: Pick two points ON the line (not necessarily data points), compute slope and intercept, and interpret. To check, ask: "A fitted line passes through (150, 150) and (180, 180) (arm span, height in cm). Write it and interpret the slope." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: A fitted line passes through (150, 150) and (180, 180) (arm span, height in cm). Write it and interpret the slope.
questions.a: Slope 30/30 = 1, so y = x: about 1 cm more height per 1 cm more arm span.

days.guide: Use a model to predict and judge reasonableness. Finish by asking: "Price model p = −0.1m + 20,000 (m = miles). Predict at 80,000 miles. Is 250,000 miles reasonable?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Price model p = −0.1m + 20,000 (m = miles). Predict at 80,000 miles. Is 250,000 miles reasonable?
questions.a: At 80,000: −8,000 + 20,000 = $12,000. At 250,000 the model gives −$5,000, which is impossible — too far beyond the data.

days.guide: Teach residual = actual − predicted. Child computes 5 residuals for two lines and compares; check with Desmos regression (y1 ~ mx1 + b).

questions.q: Actual height 165 cm, predicted 162 cm. Residual?
questions.a: +3 cm (the point is 3 cm above the line).

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: A model of test score vs study hours is y = 5x + 60. Interpret 5 and 60.
questions.a: Each extra hour of study is associated with about 5 more points; 60 is the predicted score with 0 hours.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz rubric: line drawn through the middle of the cloud (2), equation from two points on the line correct (2), slope interpreted with units, e.g., 'about 1 cm of height per cm of arm span' (2), intercept interpreted or noted as not meaningful (1), one prediction with reasonableness comment (1). Example: line through (150, 150) and (180, 180) → y = x.

weeks.prep: Survey sheet with two yes/no questions; calculator. Prepare the Unit 6 review and test.
misconceptions: Comparing raw counts when group sizes differ. Use relative frequencies (percents) within each row or column.
Computing the percent of the wrong total. Ask: 'percent of what?' — the row total or column total.

days.guide: Survey 20 people (or use data) and fill in a two-way table with totals. To check, ask: "Table: instrument & likes math 8; instrument & not 2; no instrument & likes math 4; no instrument & not 6. How many surveyed? How many like math?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Table: instrument & likes math 8; instrument & not 2; no instrument & likes math 4; no instrument & not 6. How many surveyed? How many like math?
questions.a: 20 surveyed; 12 like math.

days.guide: Compute row percents and compare. Finish by asking: "Using that table, is there an association?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Using that table, is there an association?
questions.a: Yes: 8/10 = 80% of instrument players like math vs 4/10 = 40% of non-players — a big difference.

days.guide: Child analyzes 3 data sets and writes claims with relative-frequency evidence. Before moving on, ask: "If 60% of teens with a curfew do chores and 58% without a curfew do chores, is there an association?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: If 60% of teens with a curfew do chores and 58% without a curfew do chores, is there an association?
questions.a: Little or none — the percents are nearly equal.

days.guide: Mixed review: scatter plots, lines of fit, two-way tables. Check understanding with: "Line through (2, 10) and (6, 22). Equation?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Line through (2, 10) and (6, 22). Equation?

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test. To check, ask: "Does a strong association prove one variable causes the other?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Does a strong association prove one variable causes the other?
questions.a: No — a third factor or coincidence may explain it.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test suggested items: 1) Describe a scatter plot (direction, form, strength, outliers). 2) Line through (2, 10) and (6, 22) → y = 3x + 4. 3) Predict y at x = 8 → 28. 4) Residual if actual is 30 → +2. 5) Two-way table: instrument yes: 8 like math, 2 don't; no: 4 like, 6 don't → 80% vs 40%, so there is an association. 6) Explain why association ≠ causation. 1–3 points each.

weeks.prep: Several sheets of paper for folding; notebook.
misconceptions: Multiplying the bases: 2³ × 2⁴ = 4⁷. The base stays the same; only exponents add.
Adding exponents for a power of a power: (5²)³ = 5⁵. Expand to see it is 5⁶.

days.guide: Fold a sheet in half repeatedly, recording layers: 2, 4, 8 ... as powers of 2. Finish by asking: "How many layers after 10 folds?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: How many layers after 10 folds?

days.guide: Expand 10³ × 10⁴ into factors and count. Child states the rule and practices 12.

questions.q: Simplify 2⁵ × 2³ and evaluate.
Why don't you multiply the exponents in a^m × a^n?
questions.a: Writing out the factors shows m factors of a followed by n more, for m + n factors in total.

days.guide: Expand (5²)³ as 5² · 5² · 5² to see 5⁶. Check understanding with: "Simplify (5²)³." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Simplify (5²)³.

days.guide: Expand 7⁶ / 7² and cancel to see 7⁴. Child solves 12 mixed problems.

questions.q: Simplify 7⁶ ÷ 7².

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: Simplify (4²)³ ÷ 4⁵.

weeks.prep: Notebook; make a 20-card exponent sort (10 pairs of equivalent expressions).
misconceptions: Thinking a negative exponent makes a number negative. 10⁻² = 1/100, a small positive number.
Thinking a⁰ = 0. Use the pattern (each step down divides by a) to show a⁰ = 1.

days.guide: Table: 10³ = 1000, 10² = 100, 10¹ = 10; each step divides by 10, so 10⁰ = 1. Repeat with base 2.

questions.q: Why is 10⁰ = 1?
questions.a: Each time the exponent drops by 1 we divide by 10; 10¹ ÷ 10 = 1.

days.guide: Continue the pattern below 0. Child rewrites 10 expressions with positive exponents.

questions.q: Evaluate 10⁻² and 2⁻³.

days.guide: Show 2³ × 5³ = (2·5)(2·5)(2·5) = 10³. Child evaluates 8 expressions.

questions.q: Evaluate 2³ × 5³ and 4² × 25².

days.guide: Child completes the 20-card sort matching equivalents. Finish by asking: "Simplify 3⁻² × 3⁵." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Simplify 3⁻² × 3⁵.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: Simplify 6⁴ ÷ 6⁶.

weeks.prep: Print the NASA planetary fact sheet (nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet); calculator; number lines labeled 10⁻⁴ to 10⁸.
misconceptions: Writing 35 × 10⁴ as scientific notation. The coefficient must be at least 1 and less than 10: 3.5 × 10⁵.
Moving the decimal the wrong way for small numbers. Small numbers (less than 1) have negative exponents.

days.guide: Place 3 × 10⁵ and 7 × 10⁻³ on number lines marked with powers of 10. Check understanding with: "Between which powers of 10 is 3 × 10⁵?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Between which powers of 10 is 3 × 10⁵?
questions.a: Between 10⁵ and 10⁶.

days.guide: Model moving the decimal and counting places; child converts 12 quantities. To check, ask: "Write 93,000,000 miles (Earth–Sun distance) in scientific notation." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Write 93,000,000 miles (Earth–Sun distance) in scientific notation.
questions.a: 9.3 × 10⁷ miles.

questions.q: Write 0.00045 in scientific notation.

days.guide: Use powers of 10 to estimate ratios. Finish by asking: "Earth's mass ≈ 6 × 10²⁴ kg, the Moon's ≈ 7 × 10²² kg. About how many times more massive is Earth?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Earth's mass ≈ 6 × 10²⁴ kg, the Moon's ≈ 7 × 10²² kg. About how many times more massive is Earth?
questions.a: 6/7 × 10² ≈ 86, so roughly 80–90 times (actual ≈ 81).

days.guide: Show calculator 'E' notation (1.496E11 = 1.496 × 10¹¹). Child converts NASA data.

questions.q: What does 1.496E11 mean?
questions.a: 1.496 × 10¹¹ — Earth's average distance from the Sun in meters.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

weeks.prep: Calculator, NASA planetary distance data. Prepare the self-checking review puzzle and the Unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Adding exponents when adding numbers in scientific notation. To add, first rewrite with the same power of 10, then add coefficients.
Leaving answers like 30 × 10⁷. Adjust to 3 × 10⁸.

days.guide: Multiply coefficients, add exponents, then fix the coefficient if needed. To check, ask: "(5 × 10⁴)(6 × 10³)?" and compare the answer with the model below.
Rewrite with a common power before adding/subtracting. Child completes 8.

Child computes light travel time = distance ÷ (3 × 10⁸ m/s) for each planet. Before moving on, ask: "Earth is 1.5 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun. How long does sunlight take?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Earth is 1.5 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun. How long does sunlight take?
questions.a: 5 × 10² s = 500 s ≈ 8.3 minutes.

questions.q: Jupiter is about 7.8 × 10¹¹ m away. Light time?
questions.a: 2.6 × 10³ s ≈ 43 minutes.

days.guide: Child works the self-checking puzzle. Check understanding with: "Simplify (10³)⁻²." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Simplify (10³)⁻².

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test. To check, ask: "(3 × 10⁸)(2 × 10³)?" and compare the answer with the model below.

weeks.prep: Graph paper, ruler. Make a perfect-squares chart 1² to 15².
misconceptions: Thinking √50 ≈ 25. Square root asks 'what times itself', not 'half of'.
Forgetting x² = p has two solutions. x² = 81 → x = 9 or −9.

days.guide: Child draws a tilted square with vertices (0,0), (3,1), (2,4), (−1,3) and finds the area by surrounding it with a 4×4 square and subtracting four triangles. Finish by asking: "Area of that tilted square?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Area of that tilted square?
questions.a: 16 − 4(1.5) = 10 square units.

days.guide: Side length is √(area). Child writes side lengths as square roots and estimates.

questions.q: Between which two whole numbers is √10?
questions.a: 3 and 4 (closer to 3, since 9 < 10 < 16).

days.guide: Drill perfect squares 1–225. Solve x² = p for 10 values.

questions.q: Solve x² = 81 and x² = 20.

days.guide: Estimate by squaring guesses to the tenth. To check, ask: "Estimate √50, √72 and √130 to the tenth." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Estimate √50, √72 and √130 to the tenth.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: Place √30 on a number line.
questions.a: Between 5 and 6, about 5.5 (5.48).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Tilted square with side from (0,0) to (3,1): area 10, side √10. 2) Tilted square side from (0,0) to (2,2): area 8, side √8. 3) x² = 81 → ±9. 4) x² = 20 → ±√20 ≈ ±4.47. 5) x² = 144 → ±12. 6) Place √10 (≈3.16), √30 (≈5.48), √2 (≈1.41) on a number line. 7) √50 between 7 and 8 (≈7.07).

weeks.prep: Graph paper, scissors, ruler, a long string with 12 equally spaced knots (for a 3-4-5 triangle).
misconceptions: Adding legs then squaring: (a + b)² instead of a² + b². Square each first.
Using a² + b² = c² where c isn't the longest side. c is always the hypotenuse, opposite the right angle.

days.guide: Draw right triangles on grid, build squares on each side, record areas. Before moving on, ask: "For a 3-4-5 right triangle, what are the areas of the squares?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: For a 3-4-5 right triangle, what are the areas of the squares?

days.guide: Cut four congruent right triangles and arrange them in an (a + b) square two ways. Check understanding with: "Explain the 'two squares' proof." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Explain the 'two squares' proof.
questions.a: Both big squares have side a + b and contain the same four triangles. The uncovered area is c² in one and a² + b² in the other, so a² + b² = c².

days.guide: Child solves 10 missing-side problems, leaving answers as square roots and decimals. To check, ask: "Legs 6 and 8: hypotenuse?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Legs 6 and 8: hypotenuse?
Hypotenuse 13, leg 5: other leg?
Legs 5 and 7?

days.guide: Test triples with the converse; check a room corner with the 3-4-5 knotted string. Finish by asking: "Is 6-7-9 a right triangle?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Is 6-7-9 a right triangle?

days.guide: Give the quiz plus written proof explanation. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: Is 5-12-13 a right triangle?

weeks.assessment_key: Proof explanation rubric (4 levels): 4 = describes a square of side a + b containing four congruent right triangles; the leftover area is c² in one arrangement and a² + b² in the other, so a² + b² = c²; 3 = correct idea with a gap; 2 = describes the picture without the area reasoning; 1 = restates the formula only. Quiz: 1) legs 6, 8 → 10. 2) legs 5, 7 → √74 ≈ 8.60. 3) hyp 13, leg 5 → 12. 4) legs 2, 3 → √13 ≈ 3.61. 5) Is 5-12-13 right? Yes (25 + 144 = 169). 6) Is 6-7-9 right? No (36 + 49 = 85 ≠ 81).

weeks.prep: A rectangular box (shoe box), tape measure, straw or string, graph paper. Measure a TV's width, height and diagonal.
misconceptions: Forgetting to square-root at the end. a² + b² gives c², not c.
Using the face diagonal instead of the space diagonal in 3-D. Do two steps: face diagonal first, then use it with the height.

days.guide: Model the ladder problem and measure a TV. Check understanding with: "A 13-ft ladder's base is 5 ft from the wall. How high does it reach?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: A 13-ft ladder's base is 5 ft from the wall. How high does it reach?
A TV screen is 48 × 27 in. Diagonal?

days.guide: Compute the shoe box's space diagonal in two steps and check with a straw. To check, ask: "Box 30 × 18 × 12 cm. Space diagonal?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Box 30 × 18 × 12 cm. Space diagonal?

days.guide: Draw the right triangle under the segment; legs are differences of coordinates. Finish by asking: "Distance from (1, 2) to (4, 6)?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Distance from (1, 2) to (4, 6)?
questions.a: Legs 3 and 4, distance 5.

questions.q: Distance from (−2, 1) to (3, −3)?

days.guide: Child solves 6 multi-step problems. Before moving on, ask: "A park is 300 m by 400 m. How much shorter is walking the diagonal than walking around two sides?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: A park is 300 m by 400 m. How much shorter is walking the diagonal than walking around two sides?
questions.a: Diagonal 500 m vs 700 m: 200 m shorter.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: Space diagonal of a 10-cm cube?

weeks.prep: Sugar cubes or snap cubes (at least 64), calculator.
misconceptions: Confusing cube root with dividing by 3. ∛27 = 3 because 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, not 27 ÷ 3.
Thinking every decimal that goes on forever is irrational. Repeating decimals are rational.

days.guide: Build cubes of side 1–5 and count small cubes. Solve x³ = p.

questions.q: Solve x³ = 64.
Estimate ∛30.
questions.a: Between 3 (27) and 4 (64), about 3.1.

days.guide: Long division of 5/11 and 7/12; mark repeating parts. Finish by asking: "Write 5/11 and 7/12 as decimals." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Write 5/11 and 7/12 as decimals.

days.guide: Model: x = 0.777..., 10x = 7.777..., subtract: 9x = 7. Before moving on, ask: "Convert 0.2727... to a fraction." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Convert 0.2727... to a fraction.
Convert 1.1666...

days.guide: Child sorts 16 numbers into rational/irrational with justification. Check understanding with: "Classify √16, π, 0.1212..., √2, 22/7." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.a: √16 = 4 rational; π irrational; 0.1212... = 4/33 rational; √2 irrational; 22/7 rational (it only approximates π).

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review & check day: have the child redo any missed problem in the notebook and explain the error in one sentence.

questions.q: Convert 0.777... to a fraction.

weeks.prep: Number line strips, calculator (for checking only Monday). Prepare the Unit 8 test.
misconceptions: Thinking 22/7 equals π. It is a rational approximation (3.142857...).
Ordering numbers by looking at the radicand only. Convert each to a decimal approximation first.

days.guide: Trap √2 with successive number lines. Finish by asking: "Between which tenths and hundredths is √2?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Between which tenths and hundredths is √2?

days.guide: Convert each number to a decimal and order on a number line. Before moving on, ask: "Order π, √10, 3.1, 22/7, 3.15." and have the child point to evidence or show work.
Estimate then check with calculator. Check understanding with: "Estimate π² and 2√5 + 1." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Estimate π² and 2√5 + 1.

days.guide: Mixed review of the unit. To check, ask: "Distance from (−1, −1) to (5, 7)?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Distance from (−1, −1) to (5, 7)?
questions.a: Legs 6 and 8: 10.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test. Finish by asking: "Is √50 rational?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Is √50 rational?
questions.a: No — 50 is not a perfect square, so √50 is irrational (≈ 7.07).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test suggested items: 1) √2 is between 1.41 and 1.42. 2) Order π, √10, 3.1, 22/7, 3.15 → 3.1 < π < 22/7 < 3.15 < √10. 3) Legs 9, 12 → 15. 4) Distance (−1, −1) to (5, 7) → 10. 5) Is 8-15-17 right? Yes. 6) ∛216 = 6. 7) 0.4545... = 5/11. 8) Estimate 2√5 + 1 ≈ 5.47. 9) Classify √49 (rational) and √50 (irrational). 1–2 points each.

weeks.prep: Measuring tape, calculator, a ping-pong ball or marble; poster paper and markers.
misconceptions: Demanding an exact answer. A Fermi estimate aims for the right order of magnitude with stated assumptions.
Forgetting unit consistency (meters vs centimeters). Convert everything before multiplying.

days.guide: Measure the living room; estimate how many 4-cm ping-pong balls fit. Before moving on, ask: "Room 5 m × 4 m × 2.5 m; ball volume ≈ 33.5 cm³. Estimate." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Room 5 m × 4 m × 2.5 m; ball volume ≈ 33.5 cm³. Estimate.
questions.a: Room = 50 m³ = 5 × 10⁷ cm³. 5 × 10⁷ ÷ 33.5 ≈ 1.5 × 10⁶; with packing gaps (≈ 64% filled) about 1 × 10⁶ balls.

days.guide: Estimate lifetime heartbeats. Check understanding with: "At 70 beats/min for 80 years, about how many heartbeats?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: At 70 beats/min for 80 years, about how many heartbeats?

days.guide: Child picks a question, researches a few facts, builds an estimate. To check, ask: "California has about 39 million people. If each eats about 1/2 pizza per week, how many pizzas per year?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: California has about 39 million people. If each eats about 1/2 pizza per week, how many pizzas per year?

days.guide: Child presents the poster; you ask about assumptions. Finish by asking: "How do you check reasonableness?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: How do you check reasonableness?
questions.a: Compare with a known quantity or re-estimate with different assumptions; the result should be in the same order of magnitude.

days.guide: Score with the rubric together; child completes 6 cumulative review problems. Before moving on, ask: "(6 × 10⁴)(5 × 10³)?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear question, listed assumptions with sources, step-by-step calculation with units, answer in scientific notation, order-of-magnitude reasonableness check; 3 = all steps, one weak assumption or unit slip; 2 = answer with few steps or no assumptions; 1 = guess only. Cumulative review answers: give 6 items, e.g., 2³ × 2⁴ = 128; (6 × 10⁴)(5 × 10³) = 3 × 10⁸; cylinder r = 2, h = 5 → 20π ≈ 62.8; cone r = 3, h = 4 → 12π ≈ 37.7; sphere r = 1 → (4/3)π ≈ 4.19; 10⁻³ = 0.001.

weeks.prep: Desmos or a spreadsheet, graph paper; prepare a 30-problem cumulative review set.
misconceptions: Confusing profit with revenue. Profit = revenue − cost.
Thinking break-even means zero sales. It's where revenue equals cost.

days.guide: Child chooses a business and writes a cost function. Check understanding with: "Lemonade: $20 fixed (pitcher, sign) + $0.25 per cup. Cost function?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Lemonade: $20 fixed (pitcher, sign) + $0.25 per cup. Cost function?

days.guide: Write revenue; solve the system. To check, ask: "Selling for $1 per cup, find break-even." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Selling for $1 per cup, find break-even.

days.guide: Fit a line to price vs sales data and predict. Finish by asking: "Sales are 50 at $1.00 and 30 at $1.50. Predict sales at $1.25 with a line." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Sales are 50 at $1.00 and 30 at $1.50. Predict sales at $1.25 with a line.

days.guide: 30-problem cumulative review; mark items to revisit. Before moving on, ask: "Solve 4x − 7 = 2x + 9." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Solve 4x − 7 = 2x + 9.

days.guide: Child presents the plan. Check understanding with: "What is profit at 50 cups for the lemonade stand?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What is profit at 50 cups for the lemonade stand?

weeks.assessment_key: Project rubric (4 levels): 4 = cost function with fixed and per-item cost, revenue function, correct break-even point from solving the system and the graph, data-based line of fit with prediction, clear recommendation; 3 = one error; 2 = functions but no break-even or no recommendation; 1 = incomplete. Example check: cost C = 20 + 0.25x, revenue R = 1x → break-even at about 27 cups.

weeks.prep: Notebook, formula sheet, calculator; prepare a two-part cumulative final.
misconceptions: Rushing on multistep problems. Encourage writing each step and checking.
Leaving irrational answers unrounded or unlabeled. State whether the answer is exact or approximate.

days.guide: 15 geometry review problems. To check, ask: "Reflect (2, −3) over the x-axis." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Reflect (2, −3) over the x-axis.

days.guide: 15 algebra review problems. Finish by asking: "Solve 5(x − 2) = 3x + 4." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Solve 5(x − 2) = 3x + 4.

days.guide: Final exam part 1. Before moving on, ask: "Legs 7 and 24: hypotenuse?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Legs 7 and 24: hypotenuse?

days.guide: Final exam part 2. Check understanding with: "Solve y = 2x − 3 and y = −x + 6." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Solve y = 2x − 3 and y = −x + 6.

days.guide: Correct exam errors; write reflection; organize portfolio for Algebra I. To check, ask: "What does 3⁻² equal?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What does 3⁻² equal?

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam suggested items: Part 1: 1) Reflect (2, −3) over the x-axis → (2, 3). 2) Similar triangles 4, 6 and 10, x → x = 15. 3) Triangle angles 90° and 38° → 52°. 4) Legs 7 and 24 → 25. 5) Cylinder r = 3, h = 4 → 36π ≈ 113.1. 6) 0.6... = 2/3. 7) Scatter plot description. Part 2: 8) 5(x − 2) = 3x + 4 → x = 7. 9) y = 2x − 3 and y = −x + 6 → (3, 3). 10) Function? {(1, 4), (2, 4)} yes. 11) (2 × 10⁵)(4 × 10⁻²) = 8 × 10³. 12) 3⁻² = 1/9. Portfolio reflection rubric: names 3 skills with evidence (before/after work samples).

SCI.overview: Science 8 follows California's integrated model: forces and energy, gravity and space, waves, Earth's history, heredity and natural selection, finishing with an engineering capstone. Each week has a hands-on investigation with household materials; have the child predict first, record data with units in a science notebook, and explain results in claim-evidence-reasoning form. Preview PhET simulations before using them and supervise any drops, launches or kitchen chemistry.

weeks.prep: Toy car, masking tape, meter stick, stopwatch/phone timer, graph paper; a composition notebook for the science notebook. Clear a 3-meter smooth floor path. Bookmark PhET 'Forces and Motion: Basics' (phet.colorado.edu).
misconceptions: Thinking speed and velocity are the same. Velocity includes direction: 2 m/s east and 2 m/s west are the same speed but different velocities.
Reading a distance-time graph as a picture of a hill. Steepness is speed; a flat segment means stopped.

days.guide: Help the child set up a notebook (table of contents, dated entries). Roll the car past while one person stands still and another walks alongside it; each describes the motion. Explain that motion is always described relative to a reference frame.

questions.q: To you walking beside the car at the same speed, how does the car appear to move?
questions.a: It appears not to move (stationary) relative to you, though it is moving relative to the floor.

days.guide: Mark 0.5-m intervals over 3 m. The child releases or pushes the car, you time it, and the child calculates average speed = distance ÷ time for 3 trials.

questions.q: The car covers 3 m in 2.4 s. What is its average speed?
Why do 3 trials?
questions.a: To reduce the effect of random errors like reaction time; average the results.

days.guide: The child graphs distance (y) vs time (x) for the car and for a walk that includes a stop. Ask what the steepness and flat parts mean.

questions.q: What does a flat (horizontal) section mean on a distance-time graph?
questions.a: The object is stopped — time passes but distance doesn't change.

questions.q: Which is faster: a steep line or a shallow line?
questions.a: The steep line.

days.guide: Open the PhET motion screen; the child changes push direction and records speed vs velocity observations. To check, ask: "A car moves 5 m/s north, then 5 m/s south. Same speed? Same velocity?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: A car moves 5 m/s north, then 5 m/s south. Same speed? Same velocity?
questions.a: Same speed (5 m/s), different velocity because direction changed.

days.guide: Give the quiz (key) and have the child write the lab summary paragraph. Finish by asking: "At 4 m/s, how far does an object go in 6 s?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: At 4 m/s, how far does an object go in 6 s?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) A car travels 3 m in 1.5 s → 2 m/s. 2) A walker goes 100 m in 80 s → 1.25 m/s. 3) At 4 m/s, how far in 6 s? 24 m. 4) Graphs: steeper line = faster; flat line = stopped; straight line = constant speed; curve getting steeper = speeding up. Lab data/graph: table with distance, time for 3 trials, average speed (distance ÷ time) with units; labeled axes (time on x, distance on y); accurate plotting. Summary paragraph names question, method, result with a number, and one source of error (reaction time).

weeks.prep: Rubber bands (or a small spring scale), a shoe, string, a ruler, three floor surfaces (carpet, tile, wood). Bookmark the PhET tug-of-war screen.
misconceptions: Thinking an object needs a net force to keep moving. Net force changes motion; with zero net force a moving object keeps moving at constant velocity.
Adding forces in opposite directions instead of subtracting. Opposite forces subtract; the net force points toward the larger one.

days.guide: Draw arrows from the center of an object; arrow length shows strength. The child draws force diagrams for 6 situations, labeling each force.

questions.q: Draw the forces on a book resting on a table.
questions.a: Gravity (weight) pointing down and the normal force from the table pointing up, equal in size, so net force is zero.

days.guide: In PhET tug-of-war, the child predicts motion before pressing Go for 8 combinations and calculates net force each time. Check understanding with: "100 N pulls left and 150 N pulls right. Net force and motion?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: 100 N pulls left and 150 N pulls right. Net force and motion?
questions.a: 50 N to the right; the cart accelerates right.

questions.q: If the net force is zero, can the cart be moving?
questions.a: Yes — it keeps moving at constant velocity (or stays at rest).

days.guide: Tie the shoe to a rubber band; pull it slowly at steady speed across each surface and measure stretch. Keep the same shoe, same pull speed and same rubber band (controlled variables).

questions.q: Why use the same shoe on all surfaces?
questions.a: To control variables so only the surface changes.

days.guide: The child graphs stretch for each surface (bar graph), lists controlled variables, and writes a CER paragraph. Finish by asking: "Why a bar graph instead of a line graph?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why a bar graph instead of a line graph?
questions.a: Surface type is categorical, not continuous.

days.guide: Give the force-diagram quiz and collect the CER. Before moving on, ask: "What force always opposes sliding motion?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What force always opposes sliding motion?
questions.a: Friction.

weeks.assessment_key: Force-diagram quiz: 1) Book on a table: gravity down, table's normal force up, equal → net 0. 2) 30 N right and 20 N left → 10 N right. 3) 50 N and 50 N opposite → 0 N, balanced. 4) Two people pull right with 40 N and 25 N, one pulls left with 60 N → 5 N right. CER rubric (4 levels): 4 = claim answers the question; evidence cites specific measured data (numbers with units) from the lab; reasoning links evidence to the science idea; 3 = all parts, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only. Sample claim: 'Carpet produces the most friction because the rubber band stretched the most (e.g., 6 cm vs 3 cm on tile).'

weeks.prep: Index card, coin, cup; toy car, washers or coins, tape, a board-and-books ramp, meter stick, stopwatch.
misconceptions: Expecting heavier cars to roll down a ramp much faster. Gravity pulls harder on more mass, but more mass is harder to accelerate, so (ignoring friction) acceleration is about the same.
Thinking inertia is a force. Inertia is an object's resistance to changes in motion, which depends on mass.

days.guide: Place the card on a cup with a coin on top; flick the card out. The child explains why the coin drops into the cup (inertia) and writes Newton's first law.

questions.q: Why does the coin fall into the cup instead of flying off with the card?
questions.a: The coin's inertia keeps it at rest; the quick flick applies little friction force to it, so it stays put and gravity pulls it into the cup.

days.guide: Model a good plan: question, hypothesis, independent/dependent/controlled variables, numbered procedure, blank data table. The child writes the plan.

questions.q: Name the independent, dependent and two controlled variables.
questions.a: Independent: number of washers; dependent: time (and speed) down the ramp; controlled: ramp height, release point, distance, the car.

days.guide: Run 3 trials each for 0, 2, 4 and 6 washers; the child records times and calculates average speeds. Finish by asking: "If the 6-washer car's time is nearly the same as the empty car's, what does that suggest?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: If the 6-washer car's time is nearly the same as the empty car's, what does that suggest?
questions.a: Added mass doesn't much change speed down a ramp — gravity's pull increases with mass, but so does inertia.

days.guide: The child graphs average speed vs washers, then solves 8 F = ma problems. Connect: on a ramp both force and mass increase together.

questions.q: A 2-kg cart is pushed with 10 N. Acceleration?
questions.a: a = F/m = 5 m/s².

questions.q: Same 10 N on a 4-kg cart?
questions.a: 2.5 m/s² — double the mass, half the acceleration.

days.guide: The child writes the conclusion; give the quiz (key). Check understanding with: "What force gives a 5-kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s²?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What force gives a 5-kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s²?

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric (4 levels): question, hypothesis, variables (independent = washers, dependent = time/speed, controlled = ramp height, release point, distance), data table with 3 trials and averages, graph, conclusion that matches data (expected: little change in speed with added mass; small differences due to friction and timing error), sources of error. Quiz: 1) Newton's first law: an object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity unless acted on by an unbalanced force. 2) F = ma: 10 N on 2 kg → 5 m/s². 3) 3 kg accelerating at 4 m/s² → 12 N. 4) 20 N gives 4 m/s² → 5 kg. 5) Same force on double mass → half the acceleration.

weeks.prep: Balloons (3), string (5 m), straw, tape, marbles of two sizes, a ruler with a groove. Find a slow-motion crash test video (IIHS or NHTSA on YouTube).
misconceptions: Thinking action and reaction forces cancel. They act on different objects, so they don't cancel each other.
Thinking the bigger object exerts a bigger force in a collision. The forces are equal and opposite; the effects differ because masses differ.

days.guide: Thread the string through the straw, tape a balloon to it, release and measure distance for 3 inflation sizes. Identify the force pair.

questions.q: What is the force pair in the balloon rocket?
questions.a: The balloon pushes air out the back; the air pushes the balloon forward.

questions.q: Why does a bigger inflation go farther?
questions.a: More air pushed out for longer gives a larger/longer forward push.

days.guide: The child labels action-reaction pairs in 8 scenarios and explains why they don't cancel. Finish by asking: "Why don't action-reaction forces cancel?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why don't action-reaction forces cancel?
questions.a: They act on different objects; forces cancel only when they act on the same object.

days.guide: Roll marbles into each other along the groove; record same-size and different-size collisions. Before moving on, ask: "A moving marble hits an identical still marble head-on. What happens?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: A moving marble hits an identical still marble head-on. What happens?
questions.a: The moving one nearly stops and the other rolls away at about the same speed.

days.guide: Watch the crash-test video in slow motion. Discuss how seatbelts and airbags increase the time over which the dummy stops, reducing force.

questions.q: How does an airbag reduce injury?
questions.a: It increases the stopping time and spreads the force over a larger area, so the force on the person is smaller.

days.guide: Give the quiz and the two force-pair diagrams. To check, ask: "A truck hits a bug. Which feels the larger force?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: A truck hits a bug. Which feels the larger force?
questions.a: Neither — the forces are equal; the bug has far less mass, so it undergoes a huge acceleration.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) State Newton's third law: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. 2) Swimmer: pushes water back; water pushes swimmer forward. 3) Rocket: pushes gas down/back; gas pushes rocket up/forward. 4) Hammer hits nail: hammer pushes nail in; nail pushes back on hammer. 5) Truck hits bug: forces equal; bug's tiny mass gets huge acceleration. Force-pair diagrams: arrows equal length, opposite direction, on different objects. Collision notes: equal marbles — the moving marble stops and the other moves on; big hits small — both move forward, small faster; small hits big — small bounces back, big moves slowly.

weeks.prep: Raw eggs (or water balloons), straws, tape, cardboard, cotton balls, rubber bands, plastic bags. Choose a 2-m drop site with easy cleanup. Prepare the Unit 1 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the goal is a stronger (harder) shell. Softer, crushable designs work better because they increase stopping time.
Changing many things at once when iterating. Change one main feature so you know what helped.

days.guide: Define criteria (must survive a 2-m drop; mass under 100 g) and constraints (only listed materials, 30 minutes to build). The child writes both lists.

questions.q: Criteria vs constraints?
questions.a: Criteria are what a successful design must do; constraints are limits (materials, time, cost, size).

days.guide: The child sketches 3 designs and scores them in a decision matrix (cost, mass, expected protection). Before moving on, ask: "Why use a decision matrix?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why use a decision matrix?
questions.a: It compares designs fairly against the criteria instead of choosing by gut feeling.

days.guide: Build and drop. Observe and record whether the egg survived and how the device changed during impact.

questions.q: Why does padding protect the egg?
questions.a: It increases the time it takes the egg to stop, so the force on it is smaller.

days.guide: Redesign one feature based on data, retest, and compare with another family member's design. To check, ask: "Your egg cracked on the side that hit first. What one change makes sense?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Your egg cracked on the side that hit first. What one change makes sense?
questions.a: Add more crushable padding on that side (or a parachute to reduce speed).

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test and collect the notebook pages. Finish by asking: "A 4-kg object accelerates at 2 m/s². Net force?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: A 4-kg object accelerates at 2 m/s². Net force?

weeks.assessment_key: Engineering notebook rubric (4 levels): criteria and constraints listed; 3 labeled sketches; decision matrix with scores; test data; redesign explained using evidence; reflection connects to force and collision time. Unit 1 test sample answers: speed = d/t (6 m in 3 s → 2 m/s); net force of 25 N right and 10 N left → 15 N right; F = ma (4 kg × 2 m/s² = 8 N); Newton's first law (inertia); third law pairs on different objects; crumple zones increase collision time to reduce force.

weeks.prep: A ramp (board + books), balls of different mass but similar size (golf ball, ping-pong ball, rubber ball), a paper cup with a 'door' cut in the rim, a ruler, masking tape.
misconceptions: Thinking kinetic energy doubles when speed doubles. KE depends on v², so doubling speed quadruples KE.
Thinking heavier objects always have more KE. A fast light object can have more KE than a slow heavy one.

days.guide: Brainstorm moving objects (a jogger, a bullet, a truck) and rank by kinetic energy. Introduce KE = ½mv² and units (joules).

questions.q: Rank: a slow-rolling bowling ball or a fast-thrown baseball?
questions.a: It depends on actual values; a fast baseball can have more KE because speed is squared.

days.guide: Roll balls of different mass from the same height into the cup; measure how far the cup slides. Check understanding with: "Why use the same ramp height for each ball?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Why use the same ramp height for each ball?
questions.a: So the speed at the bottom is about the same; only mass changes.

days.guide: Roll one ball from increasing heights; measure cup distance. To check, ask: "What happens to the cup distance as height increases?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What happens to the cup distance as height increases?
questions.a: It increases — more speed means more kinetic energy.

days.guide: The child graphs both data sets and calculates KE to explain why doubling speed matters more. Finish by asking: "A 2-kg ball goes 3 m/s, then 6 m/s. Compare KE." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: A 2-kg ball goes 3 m/s, then 6 m/s. Compare KE.
questions.a: 9 J vs 36 J — four times as much.

days.guide: Give the quiz (key). Before moving on, ask: "1000-kg car at 10 m/s: KE?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: 1000-kg car at 10 m/s: KE?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) KE = ½mv². 2) 2-kg ball at 3 m/s → 9 J. 3) 1000-kg car at 10 m/s → 50,000 J. 4) Same car at 20 m/s → 200,000 J (4 times). 5) 4-kg ball at 2 m/s → 8 J. Graph interpretation: mass vs KE is a straight line (proportional); speed vs KE curves upward (nonlinear). Graphs: labeled axes, two data sets, best-fit line or curve.

weeks.prep: Rubber bands, a ruler, a tray of flour or sand, a ball, magnets, paper clips, books.
misconceptions: Thinking potential energy only means height. Energy can be stored by stretching (elastic), position in a magnetic or electric field, or chemical bonds.
Forgetting that PE depends on the system (e.g., ball and Earth together).

days.guide: Drop a ball from 3 heights into flour; measure crater diameter. Check understanding with: "What does a bigger crater show?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What does a bigger crater show?
questions.a: More energy at impact — from more gravitational PE stored at greater height.

days.guide: Launch rubber bands stretched 5, 10 and 15 cm (point away from people); measure distance. To check, ask: "Why does a 15-cm stretch fly farther?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Why does a 15-cm stretch fly farther?
questions.a: More stretch stores more elastic PE, which becomes more KE.

days.guide: Bring a paper clip slowly toward a magnet and measure the jump distance; draw how arrangement changes stored energy. Finish by asking: "When is magnetic PE greatest between a magnet and paper clip?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: When is magnetic PE greatest between a magnet and paper clip?
questions.a: When they are held apart (separated), since the attraction can do work as they come together.

days.guide: The child draws before/after energy models for a roller coaster, a bow and arrow, and two magnets. Before moving on, ask: "Describe energy in a bow and arrow." and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Describe energy in a bow and arrow.
questions.a: Elastic PE in the drawn bow becomes KE of the arrow.

days.guide: Give the quiz (key). Check understanding with: "Calculate GPE of a 2-kg book on a 1.5-m shelf." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Calculate GPE of a 2-kg book on a 1.5-m shelf.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) GPE = mgh; 2-kg book on a 1.5-m shelf → 2 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 29.4 J. 2) More stretch = more elastic PE. 3) Pulling two attracting magnets apart increases PE; letting them snap together converts it to KE. 4) Roller coaster: most GPE at the top, most KE at the bottom. Model diagrams rubric: before/after pictures with energy bars or labels for each energy type and a statement that total energy is conserved (some becomes thermal).

weeks.prep: Foam pipe insulation cut lengthwise (or paper track), marbles, tape, string, washers. Bookmark PhET 'Energy Skate Park.'
misconceptions: Thinking energy is 'used up' or lost when things slow down. Energy is conserved; it transforms into thermal energy and sound.
Thinking a ball can rise higher than its starting point without extra energy. Without added energy, it can't exceed its starting height.

days.guide: Run Energy Skate Park with bar graphs on. The child records 3 patterns (KE high at bottom, PE high at top, total constant without friction).

questions.q: What happens to the total energy bar when friction is off?
questions.a: It stays constant; KE and PE trade off.

days.guide: Build a washer pendulum; observe swings and why it stops. Finish by asking: "Why does a pendulum eventually stop?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why does a pendulum eventually stop?
questions.a: Air resistance and friction at the pivot transform its mechanical energy into thermal energy (and a little sound).

days.guide: Build a foam coaster with a loop; find the minimum start height. Before moving on, ask: "Why must the marble start higher than the top of the loop?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why must the marble start higher than the top of the loop?
questions.a: It needs extra energy as KE at the top to stay on the track, plus energy lost to friction.

days.guide: The child writes a CER on where the marble's energy went. Check understanding with: "Where does energy go as a marble slows on a flat track?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Where does energy go as a marble slows on a flat track?
questions.a: Into thermal energy (heating the track and air) and sound through friction.

days.guide: Review the CER with the rubric; give a short energy transfer quiz. To check, ask: "Name the energy transformation in a falling ball." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Name the energy transformation in a falling ball.
questions.a: Gravitational PE to KE.

weeks.assessment_key: Coaster design: marble completes the loop; minimum start height recorded (theory for a frictionless slider is 2.5 times the loop radius above the bottom; real coasters need more because of friction and rolling). CER rubric (4 levels): 4 = claim answers the question; evidence cites specific measured data (numbers with units) from the lab; reasoning links evidence to the science idea; 3 = all parts, reasoning thin; 2 = claim with vague evidence; 1 = claim only. Proficient claim: 'The marble's energy wasn't destroyed; it was transformed into thermal energy and sound by friction, so the total stayed the same.'

weeks.prep: Tennis, rubber (bouncy) and clay (or play-dough) balls; meter stick; phone with slow-motion video. Prepare the Unit 2 test.
misconceptions: Thinking a rebound shows energy was 'lost.' It was transformed into heat, sound and deformation.
Confusing elastic and inelastic collisions. Elastic: little energy transformed (objects bounce); inelastic: much transformed (objects deform or stick).

days.guide: Drop each ball from 1 m; measure rebound height; calculate percent energy retained = rebound ÷ drop × 100. Finish by asking: "A tennis ball rebounds to 55 cm from 100 cm. Percent energy retained?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: A tennis ball rebounds to 55 cm from 100 cm. Percent energy retained?
questions.a: About 55% (GPE is proportional to height).

questions.q: Where did the other 45% go?
questions.a: Thermal energy, sound and deformation of the ball and floor.

days.guide: Film collisions in slow motion; identify where energy goes. Before moving on, ask: "What does the clay ball's flattening show?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What does the clay ball's flattening show?
questions.a: Energy went into permanent deformation — an inelastic collision.

days.guide: The child creates a concept map connecting force, motion, KE, PE and energy transfer. Check understanding with: "How are force and energy connected?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: How are force and energy connected?
questions.a: A force acting over a distance transfers energy (work).

days.guide: Practice with 3 KE graph questions. To check, ask: "A KE vs speed graph curves upward. Why?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: A KE vs speed graph curves upward. Why?
questions.a: KE depends on speed squared.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test. Finish by asking: "Calculate GPE of a 5-kg object 2 m high." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Calculate GPE of a 5-kg object 2 m high.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test sample answers: KE = ½mv² (3-kg at 4 m/s → 24 J); doubling speed quadruples KE; GPE = mgh (5-kg at 2 m → 98 J); energy is conserved, transforming to thermal energy; elastic vs inelastic; data question: steeper KE vs speed curve explained by v².

weeks.prep: Bathroom scale, NASA planet fact sheet, a few balls, a stretchy sheet or fabric, marbles. Bookmark PhET 'Gravity Force Lab.'
misconceptions: Thinking heavier objects fall faster. Without air resistance all objects fall with the same acceleration.
Confusing mass and weight. Mass (kg) is amount of matter and doesn't change; weight (N) is the gravitational force and depends on location.

days.guide: Drop two objects of different mass (e.g., a book and a closed water bottle) together; they land at the same time. Discuss mass vs weight.

questions.q: Why does a feather fall slower than a hammer on Earth but not on the Moon?
questions.a: Air resistance slows the feather on Earth; the Moon has no air, so both fall together (shown by Apollo 15).

days.guide: Stretch a sheet; place a heavy ball in the middle and roll marbles. Discuss what the model shows and its limits.

questions.q: Limit of the sheet model?
questions.a: It relies on Earth's gravity pulling down on the sheet and shows 2-D only; it is just an analogy.

days.guide: Use NASA data to calculate weight on each planet; graph mass vs surface gravity. To check, ask: "If you weigh 100 lb on Earth, about how much on Mars?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: If you weigh 100 lb on Earth, about how much on Mars?
questions.a: About 38 lb (Mars gravity ≈ 0.38 × Earth's).

days.guide: Use PhET Gravity Force Lab to change masses and distance; write an argument with evidence. Finish by asking: "What happens to gravitational force if one mass doubles?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What happens to gravitational force if one mass doubles?
questions.a: The force doubles.

days.guide: Give the quiz (key). Before moving on, ask: "Does your mass change on the Moon?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Does your mass change on the Moon?
questions.a: No — only your weight changes.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument rubric: claim that gravitational force depends on the masses (and distance); evidence from planet data (more massive planets generally have stronger surface gravity, e.g., Jupiter 24.8 m/s² vs Earth 9.8 vs Mars 3.7) and the PhET sim (doubling a mass doubles the force); reasoning. Quiz: mass stays the same on the Moon; 100 lb on Earth ≈ 38 lb on Mars and ≈ 17 lb on the Moon; gravity is always attractive; force decreases with distance.

weeks.prep: A lamp without a shade, a foam ball on a pencil, a dark room, a moon observation chart. Check tonight's moon phase (e.g., timeanddate.com).
misconceptions: Thinking Earth's shadow causes moon phases. Phases come from how much of the sunlit half we see; Earth's shadow only matters in lunar eclipses.
Thinking eclipses should happen every month. The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so the Sun, Earth and Moon line up only at certain times.

days.guide: Start the 14-day moon log tonight; research tonight's phase. Check understanding with: "Where should you record each observation?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Where should you record each observation?
questions.a: Date, time, shape sketch, and position in the sky.

days.guide: In a dark room, hold the ball at arm's length and turn in a circle around the lamp; sketch the lit part at 8 positions. To check, ask: "When the ball is between you and the lamp, what phase do you see?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: When the ball is between you and the lamp, what phase do you see?
questions.a: New moon — the lit side faces away.

days.guide: Order phase photos; explain why we always see the same side. Finish by asking: "Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
questions.a: It rotates once for each orbit (about 27 days), so the same face points toward Earth.

days.guide: Use the lamp model to show solar and lunar eclipses. Before moving on, ask: "Why don't eclipses happen every month?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why don't eclipses happen every month?
questions.a: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's orbit, so it usually passes above or below the Sun-Earth line.

days.guide: Give the quiz; update the moon log. Check understanding with: "During which phase can a solar eclipse occur?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: During which phase can a solar eclipse occur?
questions.a: New moon.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz answers: phases in order: new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, third (last) quarter, waning crescent; cycle ≈ 29.5 days; solar eclipse: Moon between Sun and Earth at new moon; lunar eclipse: Earth between Sun and Moon at full moon; umbra = darkest part of a shadow. Sketch rubric: 8 phases correctly shaded and labeled.

weeks.prep: Flashlight, graph paper, a globe or ball with an axis, a lamp, sunrise/sunset data for your city and a Southern Hemisphere city (timeanddate.com).
misconceptions: Thinking seasons are caused by Earth's distance from the Sun. Earth is closest in early January — during Northern Hemisphere winter.
Thinking the tilt changes direction. The axis stays pointed toward the North Star as Earth orbits.

days.guide: The child writes what causes seasons, then examines Earth-Sun distance data. To check, ask: "When is Earth closest to the Sun?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: When is Earth closest to the Sun?
questions.a: Early January (about 147 million km).

days.guide: Shine the flashlight straight down and at an angle onto graph paper; count lit squares. Finish by asking: "Why is angled light weaker?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why is angled light weaker?
questions.a: The same energy spreads over a larger area.

days.guide: Graph day length for both cities. Before moving on, ask: "How do the graphs compare?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How do the graphs compare?
questions.a: They are opposites: when one has long days, the other has short.

days.guide: Walk the tilted globe around the lamp. Check understanding with: "At the June solstice, which hemisphere tilts toward the Sun?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: At the June solstice, which hemisphere tilts toward the Sun?
questions.a: Northern.

days.guide: Write the seasons explanation; give the quiz. To check, ask: "What causes seasons?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What causes seasons?
questions.a: Earth's tilted axis.

weeks.assessment_key: Seasons explanation rubric: Earth's 23.5° tilt means each hemisphere receives more direct sunlight and longer days in its summer and less direct sunlight and shorter days in winter; references flashlight lab (same light spread over more area at an angle) and day-length data; addresses the distance misconception. Quiz: solstices ~June 21 and ~December 21; equinoxes ~March 20 and ~September 22 (about 12 hours of day everywhere); Southern Hemisphere has opposite seasons.

weeks.prep: String, a soft ball or eraser, open outdoor space; PhET 'Gravity and Orbits'; NASA galaxy images (nasa.gov / hubblesite.org).
misconceptions: Thinking there's no gravity in space. Astronauts in orbit are in free fall; gravity there is still about 90% of surface gravity.
Thinking orbiting objects need a push to keep moving. Inertia keeps them moving; gravity curves the path.

days.guide: Swing the ball on a string in a circle and release it (outdoors, safely). Note it flies off in a straight line.

questions.q: What does the string represent?
questions.a: Gravity — the inward pull that keeps the object curving.

days.guide: In the sim, turn gravity off and change masses; record effects. Before moving on, ask: "What happens when gravity is turned off?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What happens when gravity is turned off?
questions.a: The planet moves off in a straight line.

days.guide: Read about the solar nebula; draw a 4-panel model. Check understanding with: "How did the Sun form?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: How did the Sun form?
questions.a: Gravity pulled the center of a spinning gas cloud together until it was hot enough for fusion.

days.guide: Explore galaxy images; explain gravity's role. To check, ask: "About how many stars are in the Milky Way?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: About how many stars are in the Milky Way?
questions.a: Roughly 100–400 billion.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Finish by asking: "Why doesn't the Moon fly away?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why doesn't the Moon fly away?
questions.a: Earth's gravity pulls it inward.

weeks.assessment_key: Formation model rubric: 4 panels — a rotating cloud of gas and dust (solar nebula); gravity pulls it inward and it spins faster and flattens into a disk; the Sun forms in the hot center; planets form by accretion of particles. Quiz: an orbit results from inertia (forward motion) plus gravity (pull toward center); without gravity an orbiting object moves off in a straight line; the Milky Way is a spiral galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars held by gravity.

weeks.prep: Toilet paper roll, marker, calculator, NASA planet fact sheet, hallway or outdoor space. Prepare the Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Thinking textbook diagrams show true scale. Planets are tiny and far apart; diagrams compress distances.
Thinking a light-year is time. It's a distance (about 9.5 trillion km).

days.guide: Compare diameters: Earth 12,756 km, Jupiter 142,984 km, Sun ~1,392,700 km. Before moving on, ask: "How many Earths fit across Jupiter? Across the Sun?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: How many Earths fit across Jupiter? Across the Sun?
questions.a: About 11 across Jupiter and about 109 across the Sun.

days.guide: Unroll the toilet paper; mark planets at their squares. Check understanding with: "Where is Earth?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Where is Earth?
questions.a: About 15 squares from the Sun.

days.guide: Explain why one model can't show both size and distance. To check, ask: "If Earth is a 2-mm peppercorn, how far from the Sun?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: If Earth is a 2-mm peppercorn, how far from the Sun?
questions.a: About 23.5 m, with a Sun about 22 cm wide.

days.guide: Review with a study guide. Finish by asking: "What is an AU?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What is an AU?
questions.a: Earth-Sun average distance, about 150 million km.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test. Before moving on, ask: "What is a light-year?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What is a light-year?
questions.a: The distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion km.

weeks.assessment_key: Scale model rubric: planets placed at correct squares (1 square ≈ 10 million km): Mercury ~6, Venus ~11, Earth ~15, Mars ~23, Jupiter ~78, Saturn ~143, Uranus ~287, Neptune ~450 squares. Unit 3 test sample answers: gravity depends on mass and distance; phases from viewing angle of the sunlit half; solar eclipse at new moon, lunar at full; seasons from tilt; orbits from inertia + gravity; 1 AU ≈ 150 million km.

weeks.prep: A Slinky or long rope, a ruler, a pan of water, pebbles. Bookmark PhET 'Wave on a String.'
misconceptions: Thinking the material travels with the wave. Waves carry energy; the medium only vibrates in place.
Thinking higher frequency means faster waves. In the same medium speed is constant; higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

days.guide: Make transverse and longitudinal waves with the Slinky; sketch and label. Check understanding with: "Which kind of wave is sound?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Which kind of wave is sound?
questions.a: Longitudinal.

days.guide: In PhET, change amplitude and frequency; measure wavelength. To check, ask: "What happens to wavelength as frequency increases?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: What happens to wavelength as frequency increases?
questions.a: It decreases.

days.guide: Drop a pebble from different heights; observe wave height. Finish by asking: "What does greater amplitude mean?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What does greater amplitude mean?
questions.a: More energy.

days.guide: Teach v = fλ; the child solves 8 problems. Before moving on, ask: "v = 340 m/s, f = 170 Hz. Wavelength?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: v = 340 m/s, f = 170 Hz. Wavelength?

days.guide: Give the quiz. Check understanding with: "Define wavelength." If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Define wavelength.
questions.a: Distance from one crest to the next.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: label crest, trough, wavelength (crest to crest), amplitude (rest to crest). v = fλ: 1) f = 5 Hz, λ = 2 m → 10 m/s. 2) v = 340 m/s, f = 170 Hz → λ = 2 m. 3) v = 12 m/s, λ = 3 m → f = 4 Hz. 4) Transverse = vibrations perpendicular to wave direction (rope); longitudinal = parallel (sound, Slinky push).

weeks.prep: Paper cups, string, rubber bands, a tissue box, 4–5 identical glasses, water, a spoon, towels, foam, cardboard; install a free decibel-meter app.
misconceptions: Thinking sound travels best through air. Sound travels faster and often more clearly through solids and liquids, and not at all through a vacuum.
Confusing pitch with loudness. Pitch depends on frequency; loudness on amplitude.

days.guide: Pluck rubber bands over a tissue box; change tension and length and record pitch. To check, ask: "How does tightening a rubber band change pitch?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: How does tightening a rubber band change pitch?
questions.a: Higher pitch — it vibrates at a higher frequency.

days.guide: Make a cup-and-string telephone; compare transmission through string, air and a table. Finish by asking: "Why does the string phone work only when the string is tight?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why does the string phone work only when the string is tight?
questions.a: The vibrations travel through the taut string; a slack string doesn't transmit them well.

days.guide: Tap glasses filled to different levels; explain pitch differences. Before moving on, ask: "Which glass makes the lowest pitch when tapped?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Which glass makes the lowest pitch when tapped?
questions.a: The fullest — more water makes the glass vibrate more slowly (lower frequency).

days.guide: Play the same sound through each material and measure decibels with the app. Check understanding with: "Why keep phone volume and distance the same?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Why keep phone volume and distance the same?
questions.a: To control variables so only the material changes.

days.guide: Give the quiz and collect the absorption write-up. To check, ask: "Can sound travel through space?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Can sound travel through space?
questions.a: No — there's no medium.

weeks.assessment_key: Investigation report rubric (4 levels): question; hypothesis; controlled variables (same phone, volume, distance, sound); data table of decibel readings for each material with 3 trials; graph; conclusion (soft, porous materials like towels and foam usually absorb the most sound); sources of error. Quiz: pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude; sound needs a medium; tighter or shorter band → higher pitch.

weeks.prep: Flashlight, mirror, protractor, glass of water, pencil, coin, opaque cup, wax paper, aluminum foil, clear plastic, cardboard. Bookmark PhET 'Bending Light.'
misconceptions: Measuring reflection angles from the mirror's surface. Angles are measured from the normal (a line perpendicular to the surface).
Thinking refraction happens because light 'bends inside' water. It changes direction at the boundary because its speed changes.

days.guide: Shine the flashlight through each material; classify. Finish by asking: "Wax paper lets some light through but blurs it. Category?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Wax paper lets some light through but blurs it. Category?
questions.a: Translucent.

days.guide: Test the law of reflection with mirror, flashlight and protractor. Before moving on, ask: "Light hits a mirror at 40° from the normal. Reflection angle?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Light hits a mirror at 40° from the normal. Reflection angle?

days.guide: Observe a pencil in water and the 'appearing coin' trick; draw ray diagrams. Check understanding with: "Why does the coin appear when water is added?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Why does the coin appear when water is added?
questions.a: Light from the coin refracts at the water's surface and bends toward your eye.

days.guide: Use Bending Light to change materials and record ray paths. To check, ask: "When light enters a slower material at an angle, which way does it bend?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: When light enters a slower material at an angle, which way does it bend?
questions.a: Toward the normal.

days.guide: Give the ray-diagram quiz. Finish by asking: "State the law of reflection." — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: State the law of reflection.
questions.a: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.

weeks.assessment_key: Ray diagram quiz: 1) Reflection: draw incident ray, normal, reflected ray; angle of incidence = angle of reflection (e.g., 30° in → 30° out). 2) Refraction from air into water: ray bends toward the normal. 3) From water into air: bends away from the normal. 4) Classify: clear plastic transparent, wax paper translucent, foil and cardboard opaque.

weeks.prep: A prism or glass of water, sunny window, white paper, red and blue cellophane, flashlight, colored objects. Prepare the semester exam (Units 1–4).
misconceptions: Thinking objects 'have' color. An object reflects certain wavelengths and absorbs the rest; color depends on the light.
Mixing up light and paint (pigment) color rules.

days.guide: Make a spectrum with a prism or water glass in sunlight. Before moving on, ask: "Why does white light separate?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Why does white light separate?
questions.a: Different wavelengths refract by different amounts; violet bends most, red least.

days.guide: View colored objects through red and blue cellophane. Check understanding with: "A blue object through red cellophane looks how?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: A blue object through red cellophane looks how?
questions.a: Dark/black — the red filter blocks the blue light it reflects.

days.guide: Review forces and energy with a practice test. To check, ask: "Net force: 15 N right, 5 N left?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Net force: 15 N right, 5 N left?
questions.a: 10 N right.

days.guide: Review space and waves with a concept map. Finish by asking: "What causes a lunar eclipse?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: What causes a lunar eclipse?
questions.a: Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon.

days.guide: Give the semester exam. Before moving on, ask: "What is the order of colors in the spectrum?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What is the order of colors in the spectrum?
questions.a: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam sample answers: speed = d/t; net force; F = ma; Newton's three laws; KE = ½mv²; GPE = mgh; energy conservation; gravity and mass; phases, eclipses, seasons; wave parts and v = fλ; reflection and refraction; red object under blue light looks dark. Score by percent; 80% proficient.

weeks.prep: Flashlight, paper, pencil, phone. Prepare the Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Thinking digital is always higher quality. Digital is more reliable to copy and transmit, but quality depends on sampling rate and compression.
Thinking Wi-Fi and cell signals are sound waves. They are electromagnetic (radio) waves.

days.guide: Agree on a binary code (e.g., short blink = 0, long blink = 1); send a 3-letter message with a flashlight. Check understanding with: "What number is 101 in binary?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What number is 101 in binary?
What caused errors?
questions.a: Noise — mistiming, missed blinks.

days.guide: Read about records, cassettes and digital audio; make a T-chart. To check, ask: "Advantage of digital?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Advantage of digital?
questions.a: Copies without degradation; easy to store, compress, transmit.

days.guide: Play telephone with a spoken message vs a numeric code. Finish by asking: "Why did the code survive better?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Why did the code survive better?
questions.a: Discrete digits are easier to transmit accurately than continuous speech.

days.guide: Read about cell phones and Wi-Fi; summarize. Before moving on, ask: "What carries cell phone signals?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: What carries cell phone signals?
questions.a: Radio waves (electromagnetic).

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test. Check understanding with: "Analog vs digital?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: Analog vs digital?
questions.a: Analog is continuous; digital uses discrete values.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test sample answers: label wave parts; v = fλ; sound needs a medium; light reflection/refraction; transparent/translucent/opaque; analog = continuous signal, digital = discrete values (often 0s and 1s); digital signals resist noise because receivers only need to tell 0 from 1; binary 101 = 5; cell phones use radio waves to carry digitized data.

weeks.prep: Clear jar with lid, sand, soil, gravel, water; colored play-dough; small objects as 'fossils'; clear straws.
misconceptions: Thinking the top layer is oldest. By superposition, in undisturbed layers the bottom is oldest.
Thinking a fault or intrusion is older than the layers it cuts. Whatever cuts across layers is younger.

days.guide: Pour sand, soil and gravel into water in stages; let settle. To check, ask: "Which settles first?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Which settles first?
questions.a: Gravel (largest, heaviest particles).

days.guide: Build play-dough layers with fossils and a fault; core-sample with a straw. Finish by asking: "Which layer is oldest?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Which layer is oldest?
questions.a: The bottom one (if undisturbed).

days.guide: Order events in 4 diagrams with intrusions and faults. Before moving on, ask: "An igneous intrusion cuts through layers A–C. Older or younger?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: An igneous intrusion cuts through layers A–C. Older or younger?
questions.a: Younger than A–C.

days.guide: Correlate layers from three sites using index fossils. Check understanding with: "What makes a good index fossil?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: What makes a good index fossil?
questions.a: Widespread, easily recognized, and lived for a short time.

days.guide: Give the sequencing quiz. To check, ask: "State the law of superposition." and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: State the law of superposition.
questions.a: In undisturbed layers, the oldest is at the bottom.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: sequence two cross sections (accept sequences matching your diagrams); rules applied: superposition (oldest at bottom), cross-cutting relationships (intrusions/faults are younger than layers they cut), index fossils correlate layers of the same age.

weeks.prep: 5 m of adding-machine tape or toilet paper, meter stick, markers; 100 coins or M&Ms and a container.
misconceptions: Thinking humans and dinosaurs lived together. Non-avian dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago; humans appeared about 300,000 years ago.
Thinking half-life means half the time remains. It's the time for half the atoms to decay.

days.guide: Make the 4.6-m timeline; mark events. Finish by asking: "Where is the dinosaur extinction on a 4.6-m timeline?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: Where is the dinosaur extinction on a 4.6-m timeline?
questions.a: 6.6 cm from the present end.

days.guide: Research the 5 mass extinctions and add them. Before moving on, ask: "Which was largest?" and have the child point to evidence or show work.

questions.q: Which was largest?
questions.a: End-Permian, about 252 million years ago.

days.guide: Shake coins; remove 'decayed' ones; repeat and graph. Check understanding with: "After 3 half-lives, what fraction remains?" If the answer misses the key idea, revisit today's model together.

questions.q: After 3 half-lives, what fraction remains?

days.guide: Write a scientific explanation of how strata build the time scale. To check, ask: "Relative vs absolute dating?" and compare the answer with the model below.

questions.q: Relative vs absolute dating?
questions.a: Relative orders events; absolute gives an age in years (radiometric).

days.guide: Give the quiz. Finish by asking: "How old is Earth?" — look for the specific points in the model answer.

questions.q: How old is Earth?
questions.a: About 4.6 billion years.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline: 4.6 m at 1 mm = 1 million years; first life ~3.5–3.8 billion years ago (3.5–3.8 m from present end); Cambrian explosion ~541 mya (54 cm); dinosaurs appear ~230 mya (23 cm); non-avian dinosaurs extinct ~66 mya (6.6 cm); Homo sapiens ~0.3 mya (0.3 mm). Five mass extinctions: end-Ordovician (~445 mya), Late Devonian (~372), end-Permian (~252, largest), end-Triassic (~201), end-Cretaceous (~66).
